questions.title: Prompt layout for multiple long documents
questions.prompt:
A feature answers employee questions from six internal policy documents totaling about 80k tokens in one request. The current order is question → answer instructions → six documents, concatenated without boundaries. Questions spanning documents perform poorly. The team uses Claude and Gemini APIs and wants the **approach commonly recommended by both**. Constraints:

- Change **prompt structure only**, not request parameters or features.
- Keep **all six documents in one request** because questions may span them.

Which change is most appropriate?

options.text: Wrap each document in <document> with <source> metadata, keeping instructions and question before the documents.
Put all six documents first, each wrapped in <document> with <source> metadata, and place answer instructions and question last.
Use keyword search to select only three relevant documents, structure them with tags and metadata, and put instructions and question last.
Put all six tagged documents first and the question last, additionally enabling Claude document citations.

questions.explanation:
Two problems exist: questions precede evidence and document boundaries are missing. Both platforms recommend long context first and specific questions/instructions last. Claude recommends <document> wrappers with metadata such as <source>; Gemini recommends a bridge such as “Based on the information above” followed by the question. Prompt-only changes and retaining all six documents are decisive.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Boundaries and metadata improve, but the question remains before documents. Claude reports improved complex multidocument answers with questions last, so the common layout guidance is unmet.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Documents first, question last, and document/source tags implement guidance through structure alone while retaining every document.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Layout is right, but dropping three documents prevents cross-document questions and violates full retention.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Layout is right, but enabling citations changes document-block settings, and Gemini has no identical setting, violating prompt-only changes.

Claude also recommends quoting relevant passages before completing long-document tasks.

**References**: [Prompting best practices › Long context prompting](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Prompt design strategies › Core prompting principles](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies)

questions.title: Simplifying a prompt for reasoning models
questions.prompt: A contract-risk analysis feature moved to an OpenAI reasoning model but retained its non-reasoning prompt: “Think step by step and explain the entire reasoning process,” plus eight examples with formats somewhat mismatched to the task. Quality is disappointing. The team wants to test the **simplest recommended prompt first** without **increasing per-request latency or cost**. What should it try first?

options.text: Remove only the step-by-step instruction, retaining all eight mismatched examples as references.
Remove the step-by-step instruction and revise all eight examples to match the task, retaining them.
Remove the step-by-step instruction, shorten directions, and first test without any examples.
Keep the prompt and raise reasoning.effort to high for deeper clause analysis.

questions.explanation:
The causes are unnecessary step-by-step prompting and mismatched examples; simplest-first and no extra latency/cost are decisive. OpenAI says reasoning models reason internally, so step-by-step requests are unnecessary and may harm performance. Use concise direct prompts, test zero-shot first, and add aligned examples only if needed.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: One cause is removed, but eight mismatched examples remain; examples must align with instructions.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Both causes improve, but retaining eight examples does not start from the simplest zero-shot form.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It removes the reasoning request, simplifies instructions, and starts zero-shot.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Higher effort may improve quality but increases latency/tokens and leaves prompt causes unchanged.

For reasoning models, developer messages serve the prior system-message role. To enable Markdown, put “Formatting re-enabled” on the developer message’s first line.

**References**: [Reasoning best practices › How to prompt reasoning models effectively](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning-best-practices) · [Reasoning models › Reasoning effort](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning)

questions.title: Revise examples when output formatting varies
questions.prompt:
A classification prompt requests two lines: "Category: ... / Evidence: ..." It includes four few-shot examples, but line breaks, delimiters, and tags differ, and examples are mixed into instructions. Output format varies by request. The team uses Gemini 4 and Claude and wants **TWO revisions recommended by both platforms that change only prompt text, not request parameters**.

Which should it choose?

options.text: Make all four examples structurally identical, including tags, spaces, line breaks, and example delimiters.
Keep inconsistent examples and add more than 30 correctly formatted examples so the majority format dominates.
Keep examples unchanged and append "You must use exactly two lines, Category:/Evidence:."
Wrap examples in tags such as `<example>` to separate them from instructions.
Set Gemini 4 temperature to 0 to reduce variation between requests.

questions.explanation:
Gemini says few-shot examples primarily demonstrate response format, so their structure, XML tags, spaces, line breaks, and delimiters should be consistent. Claude recommends `<example>`/`<examples>` tags to distinguish examples from instructions. Both changes affect only prompt text.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Inconsistent examples directly cause inconsistent output; standardize them first.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Retaining inconsistent examples preserves the cause. Gemini also warns that too many examples can cause overfitting.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Explicit format instructions are useful, but unchanged examples conflict with those instructions and remain mixed into them.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Tags resolve the mixing of examples and instructions.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It changes request parameters. Moreover, Gemini 4 and Gemini 3.6 or later ignore custom temperature values and return a warning header, so it would not help.

**References**: [Prompt design strategies › Consistent formatting](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Prompting best practices › Use examples effectively](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Explanations become too short after moving to Gemini 3.6 Flash
questions.prompt:
A tutoring team switches to Gemini 3.6 Flash. Students complain that explanations are too short. Answers are complete, not truncated, but concise from the start. Each request includes about 20k tokens of textbook material. Constraints:

- Do **not substantially increase input tokens**; a few instruction lines are acceptable.
- Do **not increase thinking tokens or associated latency**.
- Keep **factual definition/date questions short and direct**.

Which revision is most appropriate?

options.text: Require detailed conceptual explanation, examples, and step-by-step solutions for every question.
Add five long ideal answers with explanations, examples, and worked steps as few-shot examples.
Raise thinking_level to "high" to obtain deeper, more detailed answers.
In system instructions, require explanations, examples, and worked steps for conceptual or solution questions, but one or two sentences for factual checks.

questions.explanation:
Token restraint, unchanged thinking, and short factual answers are decisive. Gemini 3 defaults to direct efficient responses, so documentation recommends explicitly requesting detail when needed and placing core style requirements in system instructions or at the prompt’s start. Only {{option:D}} directly addresses concise defaults within all constraints.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The mechanism is appropriate, but every question becomes long, including factual checks.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Examples demonstrate desired style, but five lengthy answers substantially increase input tokens.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: thinking_level controls reasoning quantity. Raising it increases thinking tokens and latency rather than directly fixing style.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: A few lines set length by question type without substantial input or thinking overhead, retaining concise factual answers.

Gemini 3.6 onward and Gemini 4 ignore user temperature, top_p, and top_k and return deprecation-warning headers. Remove those settings; increasing temperature is not an available way to enrich responses.

**References**: [Prompt design strategies › Core prompting principles](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Prompt design strategies › Experiment with model parameters](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Gemini thinking › Controlling thinking](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking)

questions.title: A structured-output schema returns 400
questions.prompt:
A Claude API Python SDK team already defines review output with the Pydantic model ReviewResult. It converts that model to JSON Schema for output_config.format with type: "json_schema". Adding rating bounds of 1–5 and a summary maximum of 200 characters causes 400 rejection. Requirements:

- Retain **structured-output JSON guarantees**.
- Continue **range and length validation**.
- Minimize **code changes**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Remove range/length constraints from the sent schema, then write custom validation and regeneration logic.
Send transform_schema() output with constraints moved into descriptions, then use the response without further validation.
Disable output_config.format, request JSON through the prompt, and validate with ReviewResult.model_validate_json().
Pass ReviewResult to client.messages.parse() so the SDK moves unsupported constraints into descriptions and validates responses against the original constraints.

questions.explanation:
JSON guarantees, continued constraints, minimal changes, and an existing Pydantic model are decisive. Claude structured output does not support minimum, maximum, minLength, or maxLength; unsupported features return 400. Documentation recommends client.messages.parse() with Pydantic. The validating SDK helper transforms unsupported constraints into descriptions and validates returned data against the complete original schema. Reusing the existing model minimizes changes.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It retains format and validation but adds custom validation/retry code the SDK already supplies.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: transform_schema() only returns a transformed schema; it sends no request. It avoids 400 and preserves JSON format but does not validate original range/length constraints afterward.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Changes are small and Pydantic validates constraints, but removing structured outputs loses guaranteed JSON generation.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: The recommended helper handles schema limitations, retains original validation, and preserves structured-output guarantees.

output_format was deprecated in favor of output_config.format. First use incurs grammar-compilation latency, and compiled grammars remain cached for 24 hours after last use. Strict tool use shares the same JSON Schema limits.

**References**: [Structured outputs › JSON Schema limitations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs) · [Structured outputs › How SDK transformation works](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs) · [Structured outputs › Strict tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs)

questions.title: Continue multiturn function calls without storing responses
questions.prompt:
An insurance claims assistant uses the GPT-5.6 reasoning model through OpenAI Responses API. During a consultation, it calls functions such as `get_policy` and `check_claim` across multiple turns. Requirements:

- Retention policy prohibits **storing responses or conversations on OpenAI's side**.
- History is already stored in an internal database, so **resending the full history on every request is acceptable**.
- **Preserve previous reasoning** during function-call sequences to maintain quality and token efficiency.

What is most appropriate?

options.text: Leave `store` at its default and link the previous response with `previous_response_id` to preserve reasoning items.
Create a Conversations API object for each consultation and pass its ID on every request to share turns and reasoning context.
Use `store: false` and pass all items from the previous response's `output`, including encrypted reasoning items, unchanged into the next `input`.
Use `store: false` and pass only user/assistant messages and function-call/result items selected from the internal database into the next `input`.

questions.explanation:
The key constraints are [no OpenAI-side storage] and [preserve earlier reasoning]. Permission to resend history accepts the cost of stateless operation. OpenAI says response objects are stored for 30 days by default, while `store: false` disables storage. In stateless mode with `store: false` or ZDR, reasoning output includes `encrypted_content` by default, allowing reasoning to continue when passed forward. For function calls, return all reasoning, function-call, and function-result items since the last user message. To preserve reasoning from earlier turns without storage, retain every output item and resend the full history.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: This is a concise server-state continuation method, but default storage retains response objects for 30 days.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Conversations share context across turns, sessions, and devices, but conversation objects and items persist without even the 30-day TTL, violating no storage.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It preserves encrypted reasoning without server-side response storage.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It avoids storage but drops reasoning items. The documentation says retaining them supports better results with the greatest token efficiency.

Also note: `previous_response_id` still bills all prior response input tokens in the chain, so it does not reduce input costs relative to {{option:C}}. The former `include: reasoning.encrypted_content` approach remains accepted for compatibility but is no longer required.

**References**: [Conversation state › Passing context from the previous response](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state) · [Conversation state › Using the Conversations API](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state) · [Reasoning models › Preserve reasoning without stored responses](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning) · [Reasoning models › Keeping reasoning items in context](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning)

questions.title: Reducing Claude API 429 errors
questions.prompt:
An internal document Q&A service using Claude Sonnet 5.5 through the Claude API returns 429 errors every lunchtime. Every request contains the same 150k-token document collection followed by a short question. The spend cap has not been reached, and some 429 responses include a `retry-after` header. The constraints are:

- **Maintain real-time responses**, because employees wait for answers on screen.
- **Keep the current model**, whose answer quality has already been validated.
- **Keep the entire 150k-token collection as evidence for every question**; do not select only part of it for each request.

Choose **TWO** documented responses that meet these conditions.

options.text: Use vector search to select only relevant passages for each question, reducing the input to about 20k tokens and lowering input-token usage per request.
When a 429 response includes a `retry-after` header, wait that many seconds before retrying.
Send lunchtime requests through the Message Batches API to use batch limits that are separate from standard request limits.
Apply prompt caching to the shared document collection so that input tokens read from the cache are excluded from input tokens per minute (ITPM).
Route requests to Claude Haiku 5.5 only at lunchtime to distribute load across limits assigned by model class.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are maintaining real-time responses, the current model, and the entire document collection. The Claude API documentation says to wait the number of seconds specified by a 429 response’s `retry-after` header before retrying, and explains that `cache_read_input_tokens` are excluded from ITPM for most models. Caching is particularly effective when the same 150k-token collection is repeated, and it preserves all three constraints.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Fewer input tokens per request also reduce ITPM consumption, but this violates the requirement to retain the entire collection as evidence. Questions requiring passages omitted by retrieval would lack that evidence.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: This is the documented retry method, following the server’s specified wait time.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: The Message Batches API offers separate limits and a 50% discount, but is asynchronous. Although most batches finish within an hour, they may take up to 24 hours and do not support streaming, violating the real-time requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Replacing repeated large inputs with cache reads substantially reduces ITPM consumption.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Limits are assigned by model class, so distribution may help, but switching violates the requirement to keep the current, quality-validated model.

Also note: `max_tokens` does not affect OTPM calculations; OTPM counts only output tokens actually generated, in real time. A 429 caused by a spend cap has no `retry-after` header, and retries fail until access resumes. Sudden usage increases can trigger acceleration-limit 429 errors, so ramp up traffic gradually.

**References**: [Rate limits › Rate limits](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits) · [Rate limits › Cache-aware ITPM](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits) · [Batch processing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing)

questions.title: Set thinking levels by request type within one service
questions.prompt:
A support backend using Gemini 3.6 Flash handles two request types: classifying inquiries into six categories, and writing monthly reports comparing complaints across several months. Thinking is at its default medium level. Requirements:

- Reduce **classification latency and cost**.
- **Preserve current report quality**.
- Responses **must not be truncated or empty**.
- Continue using the **validated Gemini 3.6 Flash model**.

What is most appropriate?

options.text: Set `thinking_level` to `"low"` for both request types to use one configuration.
Set `thinking_level` to `"minimal"` only for classification and retain the default for reports.
Set classification `max_output_tokens` to about 20 to force less generation.
Route classification to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, whose default thinking level is minimal.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are report quality, no truncation, and model retention. Gemini recommends minimal or low thinking for simple lookups and classification, and the default for moderately difficult comparisons. `thinking_level` is configured per request in `generation_config`, so request types can differ. Gemini 3.6 Flash supports minimal, low, medium, and high.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It reduces classification latency but also reduces thinking for multimonth reports, violating quality preservation.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It reduces thinking only for simple classification while leaving comparative work at the default.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: `max_output_tokens` is a hard combined cap on thinking and output. Hitting it during thinking produces `"incomplete"` status and truncated or empty output while thinking tokens are still billed. The documentation recommends lowering `thinking_level` instead.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Flash-Lite's minimal default may reduce latency, but changes the validated model.

**References**: [Gemini thinking › Controlling thinking](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking) · [Gemini thinking › Best practices](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking)

questions.title: Client and server tools appear in one response
questions.prompt:
A travel assistant uses Claude API with a custom `get_booking` client tool and a web-search server tool in `tools`. One response includes `get_booking` `tool_use` and a `server_tool_use` that has no result yet. The application runs `get_booking` and obtains a result. It must send the next request **without ending the turn early or causing failure**.

How should it construct the request?

options.text: Put the booking `tool_result` in a user message, followed by a text block saying "Booking checked; please continue."
Put the booking `tool_result` and an empty `tool_result` for the pending web search in the user message.
Put only the booking `tool_result` block in the user message and keep the `tools` array identical to the previous request.
Remove web search from `tools` because it is unfinished, and send only the booking `tool_result`.

questions.explanation:
Claude executes server tools internally, so the application does not return their results. When client `tool_use` and unresolved `server_tool_use` appear together, documentation requires a user message containing only client `tool_result` blocks, with the same `tools` array. Adding text ends the turn early and may cause a 400 depending on the server-tool situation.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Text after `tool_result` is allowed when the assistant turn calls only client tools. With a pending server tool, only `tool_result` blocks are allowed. Text ends the turn early and, for a directly invoked Claude server tool, produces a 400 naming that tool.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: confusing similar features)**: Client tools require returned results, but the API executes the pending server call on the next request and begins the next response with its result. The application should not fabricate it.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It matches the documented configuration.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: The same tools must remain available because the pending server call executes on the next request.

**References**: [Handle tool calls › Handling results from server tools](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls) · [Handle tool calls › Handling results from client tools](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls)

questions.title: Sequence Gemini stateless function calling
questions.prompt:
You are connecting an inventory lookup function through Gemini Interactions API. Privacy policy requires **stateless operation without server-side conversation storage**, and the model has thinking enabled. Function declarations already exist. Order the steps through the second request. Items in the second request's `input` must appear **in their array order**.

- (1) Read `name`, `arguments`, and `id` from the first response's `function_call`, then run inventory lookup in application code.
- (2) Add the first turn's model-generated `thought` and `function_call` steps unchanged to the second request's `input`.
- (3) Send user input and function declarations with `store=false`.
- (4) Append a `function_result` whose `call_id` matches the earlier `id`, and send the second request.
- (5) Put the first turn's user-input step at the beginning of the second request's `input`.

items.text: Read `name`, `arguments`, and `id` from the first response's `function_call`, then run inventory lookup in application code.
Add the first turn's model-generated `thought` and `function_call` steps unchanged to the second request's `input`.
Send user input and function declarations with `store=false`.
Append a `function_result` whose `call_id` matches the earlier `id`, and send the second request.
Put the first turn's user-input step at the beginning of the second request's `input`.

questions.explanation:
Gemini function calling follows model invocation with declarations, application execution, and result return for a final answer. Stateless mode requires `store=false` and full history on every request. The documented input order is original user input, all model-generated first-turn steps including thought and function_call unchanged, then function_result referencing call_id. Putting results before model steps or omitting thought steps violates this order.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (3) First request with `store=false` | Start stateless operation | Stateless function calling |
| 2 | (1) Read and execute `function_call` | The first response must contain the call | Application executes functions |
| 3 | (5) Original user input first | Begin reconstructing full history | First input item is original user input |
| 4 | (2) Unchanged model steps | Follow user input | Preserve thought and function_call steps |
| 5 | (4) Add `function_result` and send | Requires result and id from (1) to match call_id | Final item is function_result |

Also note: Thought steps contain signatures and must be returned unchanged in stateless mode. Documentation recommends stateful operation when conversation storage is allowed.

**References**: [Function calling › How function calling works](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/function-calling) · [Function calling › Stateless function calling](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/function-calling) · [Gemini thinking › Thought signatures](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking)

questions.title: Reducing tool-selection and input errors without renaming tools
questions.prompt:
A scheduling assistant using Claude Sonnet 5.5 through the Claude API has two problems:

- Claude frequently confuses `find_event` and `list_calendar`. Both currently have one-sentence descriptions.
- `create_event` has many optional parameters and nested objects, and date and recurrence-rule formats are frequently incorrect.

Other teams’ execution code and logging dashboards depend on the current **tool names, number of tools, and `create_event` input schema, so none of these may change.** Cache-hit rates and cost also limit **the total increase in tool definitions to about 1,000 tokens per request**. Under these conditions, the team wants **TWO documentation-recommended improvements to tool definitions**.

Which should it choose?

options.text: Combine `find_event` and `list_calendar` into one `calendar` tool and distinguish operations with an `action` parameter.
Expand each of the three tool descriptions to 3–4 sentences explaining what it does, when to use and not use it, and what each parameter means.
Add five actual conversation examples to each lookup tool’s description, providing lengthy scenarios that add about 1,000 tokens per tool.
Replace the nested date and recurrence objects in `create_event` with one free-text parameter, `schedule_text`, to reduce opportunities for formatting errors.
Add schema-compliant `input_examples` to `create_event`, showing examples that omit optional parameters and illustrate date formats.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are preserving tool names, tool count, and schema, and limiting definition growth to about 1,000 tokens. Claude documentation identifies detailed tool descriptions as the most important factor in tool performance, recommends at least 3–4 sentences per tool, and recommends `input_examples` for tools with nested objects, optional parameters, or format-sensitive inputs. Both improvements preserve the names, count, and schema with only a small increase in size.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: The documentation also recommends grouping related operations into fewer tools to reduce selection confusion, but this changes the tool names and count.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: This is a core way to reduce confusion between similar tools. Adding 3–4 sentences to each of three tools stays within the increase limit.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Richer descriptions are appropriate in principle, but about 1,000 tokens per tool means about 2,000 tokens across the two tools, exceeding the limit.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Removing nested objects may reduce formatting errors, but changes the `create_event` input schema on which execution code depends.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: This suits a format-sensitive tool with many optional parameters. Every example must conform to `input_schema`; otherwise a 400 error occurs.

Also note: To prevent inputs from violating the schema itself, `strict: true` can also be added to the tool definition. `input_examples` count as prompt tokens. On Claude Sonnet 5.5, `tool_choice` values `any` and `tool` return 400 errors, so forcing a particular tool is not available.

**References**: [Define tools › Best practices for tool definitions](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools) · [Define tools › Providing tool use examples](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools) · [Define tools › Forcing tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools)

questions.title: Connect a remote MCP server with read and write tools
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI Responses API application connects an internal ERP remote MCP server using an `mcp` tool. The server exposes 60 tools, but the app needs only three inventory reads (`get_stock`, `get_price`, `get_eta`) and `create_order`. Requirements:

- Reduce per-request **tool-definition token costs and latency**.
- Require **approval every time before `create_order` sends data to the server**.
- The three reads handle public inventory information and must run **without approval round trips**.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Set `allowed_tools` to the four tools and `require_approval` to `{"never": {"tool_names": ["get_stock", "get_price", "get_eta"]}}`.
Allow the four tools and set `require_approval` to `"never"`.
Omit `allowed_tools` and set only `require_approval` to `{"never": {"tool_names": ["get_stock", "get_price", "get_eta"]}}`.
Allow the four tools and set `require_approval` to `"always"`.

questions.explanation:
Each requirement calls for a different control. OpenAI recommends allowed_tools to import only necessary definitions because many tools increase cost and latency. Remote MCP has no per-call fee; tool-definition and call tokens are billed. Approval is required by default before data leaves for the server. The `{"never": {"tool_names": [...]}}` form bypasses approval only for selected tools. Both controls are needed.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Four definitions are imported, read tools bypass approval, and create_order retains default approval.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Definitions shrink, but create_order also bypasses approval.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Approvals are correct, but all 60 tool definitions are imported.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Writes are protected, but each read adds an approval round trip.

Also note: Each approval applies to one call. Continue with mcp_approval_response and previous_response_id. Keeping mcp_list_tools in context avoids relisting tools every turn and reduces latency.

**References**: [MCP servers › Filtering tools](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp) · [MCP servers › Approvals](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp)

questions.title: Providing a long policy PDF with many tables and charts
questions.prompt:
You are building an insurance-policy assistant using direct Claude API calls to a model with a 200k-token context window. The policy is a standard PDF with a text layer (220 pages, 14MB), containing many tables and charts. In one session, a user asks 10–15 questions about its benefit-payment tables on pages 150–170. Requirements:

- No request may be **rejected because of the page limit**.
- Benefit amounts must be read **as the exact text values embedded in the PDF**, while charts and table structures must also be read **visually**.
- Do not pay **input-token costs for pages unrelated to the questions**.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Split the PDF into four pieces of about 55 pages and send all four as `document` blocks in four requests for every question, then combine the payment-table content from the four answers.
Extract only the text layer from pages 150–170 and put it before the question as a plain-text block, relying on written descriptions of the charts.
Extract pages 150–170 into a 21-page PDF and place it before the question as a `document` block, so each page is processed as both an image and extracted text.
Render pages 150–170 as individual PNG images and place them before the question as `image` blocks, letting the model read the text and tables from the images.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are the page limit, exact text values plus visual interpretation, and no costs for unrelated pages. Claude PDF support converts each page to an image and provides the text extracted from that page alongside the image, using approximately 1,500–3,000 tokens per page. A request can contain up to 600 pages, but the limit is 100 pages when the context window is below 1M tokens. The documentation recommends putting PDFs before text and splitting large PDFs when needed. Sending only the required 21 pages as a PDF meets all three requirements.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Each piece is within the page limit and preserves both tables and text, but every question includes all 220 pages. At 1,500–3,000 tokens per page, this costs about 330,000–660,000 tokens per question, violating the prohibition on costs for unrelated pages.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: This has the lowest cost and reads exact text amounts, but without page images it cannot visually interpret charts and table structure.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Sending only the necessary pages as a PDF provides both text values and visual information. Its 21 pages satisfy the page and cost constraints.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Charts and tables remain visually readable, and costs cover only necessary pages, but the extracted text layer is absent. It cannot guarantee reading amounts as the exact text values in the PDF.

Also note: The 32MB request-size limit applies to the entire body. Repeated PDFs can be referenced using a Files API `file_id` to reduce request size. On Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud, only the base64 method is available.

**References**: [PDF support › Support requirements](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/pdf-support) · [PDF support › How PDF support works](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/pdf-support) · [PDF support › Optimize PDF processing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/pdf-support)

questions.title: Implementing internal manual search
questions.prompt:
You are building an internal-manual search chatbot with the Gemini API. There are thousands of PDF manuals (each at most 100MB, with total size within the account-tier limit), and some change weekly. Questions must support restrictions such as “2026 edition, logistics department documents only,” and answers must show which files support them. The development team has two people. Requirements:

- **Minimize operational burden**; do not introduce an indexing pipeline or vector database that the team must operate.
- **Out-of-scope documents must not be mixed into the evidence.**
- Reduce **document-token costs per question**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: For each question, select PDFs matching the year and department in code, upload and attach them using the Files API, answer with long context, and show the attached filenames as sources.
Import files into a File Search store with year and department metadata, restrict retrieval using `metadata_filter`, and show sources using `file_citation`.
Chunk and embed the manuals yourself, store them in your own vector database, filter by year and department, and append the retrieved chunks and filenames to the prompt.
Import files into a File Search store without metadata, put “use only 2026 logistics department documents” in the prompt, and show sources using `file_citation`.

questions.explanation:
Each of the three requirements rules out a different option. Gemini File Search is managed RAG that imports, chunks, and indexes files, then retrieves relevant portions for the model. Key-value metadata can be attached during import, and `metadata_filter` can restrict retrieval at query time. Responses may include `file_citation` annotations identifying source files. Only relevant retrieved portions enter the model, reducing document tokens.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It can restrict scope and show file-level sources, but all matching PDFs enter the context on every question, making document-token costs high. The team must also operate document selection and uploads for each question. Files uploaded through the Files API are deleted after 48 hours.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It combines managed retrieval, metadata filtering, and citation annotations.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It supports scope restrictions, sources, and chunk-level cost reductions, but the team must operate chunking, embedding, storage, filtering, and reindexing of weekly changes. This fails the minimum-operational-burden condition.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Operational burden is low and sources are visible, but a prompt instruction alone does not filter out files from other years or departments during retrieval. Retrieved material can include out-of-scope documents, so the second requirement is not guaranteed.

Also note: File Search charges only for indexing embeddings; storage and query-time embeddings are free. Retrieved document tokens are charged as normal context tokens. File Search cannot be combined with Google Search grounding or URL Context in the same request.

**References**: [File Search › File metadata](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/file-search) · [File Search › Citations](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/file-search) · [File Search › Limitations](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/file-search)

questions.title: Reduce storage costs without regenerating embeddings
questions.prompt:
Millions of internal-wiki vectors already exist using OpenAI `text-embedding-3-large` at its default 3072 dimensions. Two problems have emerged:

- Storage costs require **smaller vectors**, but **no embedding charges to regenerate existing vectors** are allowed.
- Some long wiki documents fail embedding requests; **their later sections must remain searchable**.

Choose **TWO** appropriate actions.

options.text: Keep only the leading dimensions of stored vectors, L2-normalize them, and apply the same transformation to query vectors.
Switch to text-embedding-3-small at 1536 dimensions and re-embed every document.
Split documents exceeding the 8192-token input limit into chunks and embed each chunk.
Set dimensions to 1024 and regenerate embeddings for all documents.
Truncate oversized documents to their first 8192 tokens before embedding.

questions.explanation:
The key constraints are no regeneration of existing vectors and retaining search coverage of later text. OpenAI generally recommends dimensions at creation time, but says existing embeddings can be shortened afterward by truncating and then normalizing. All three embedding models have an 8192-token input maximum, so longer documents must be split.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It reduces storage without regeneration. The example truncates leading dimensions and divides by the L2 norm.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Storage falls, but all documents require re-embedding; its MTEB score is also lower than large.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Chunking respects the input limit while keeping the entire document searchable.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Recommended for a new index, but here it regenerates existing vectors.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Requests succeed, but text after 8192 tokens is lost from search.

Also note: Documentation says text-embedding-3-large shortened to 256 dimensions still exceeds the MTEB performance of 1536-dimensional text-embedding-ada-002.

**References**: [Vector embeddings › Embedding models](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings) · [Vector embeddings › Reducing embedding dimensions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings)

questions.title: Reading high-resolution receipt scans and marking locations
questions.prompt:
You are building an OpenAI API feature that extracts items and amounts from scanned receipts. The scans have very high resolution and dense small print. The selected model supports every `detail` value. Requirements:

- **Accuracy when reading small-print items and amounts is the top priority.**
- Extracted amounts must be **marked with boxes on the original scan**.
- Some high-resolution scans are currently **rejected at the request stage**.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Set `detail` to `"original"`, resize images to fit processing limits before sending them, and rescale returned coordinates to the original dimensions using the resize ratio before drawing boxes.
Set `detail` to `"original"`, resize images to fit processing limits before sending them, and draw boxes directly on the original scan using the returned coordinates unchanged.
Set `detail` to `"high"`, resize images to fit processing limits before sending them, and rescale returned coordinates to the original dimensions using the resize ratio before drawing boxes.
Resize every scan to fit the limits and send it with `detail: "low"`; resend only receipts that could not be read with `"high"`, and convert coordinates using the resize ratio before drawing.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are highest reading accuracy, marking positions on the original image, and resolving request rejections. OpenAI documentation recommends `original`, when supported, for large, dense images such as OCR inputs. Images exceeding the post-processing patch limit of 30,000 are rejected rather than automatically reduced. For coordinate-sensitive tasks, the documentation recommends resizing to fit limits before submission and converting returned coordinates back to the original image.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It combines the appropriate detail level for dense text, pre-resizing to avoid rejection, and conversion to original-image coordinates.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It addresses reading and rejection, but returned coordinates refer to the resized image. Drawing them unchanged on the original misaligns the boxes, violating the original-image positioning requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It handles rejection and coordinates, but the documentation recommends `original`, rather than `high`, for large, dense images such as OCR inputs. This is not the appropriate detail level for the highest-accuracy requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It handles rejection and coordinates, but `low` is intended for broad understanding and is unsuitable for small-print reading. The documentation also states that low does not always use fewer tokens than high. Resubmissions add another step and conflict with the accuracy-first requirement.

Also note: Resizing preserves aspect ratio and does not upscale small images. Supported formats are PNG, JPEG, WEBP, and non-animated GIF. Even `original` may downsize an image to meet a model’s pixel limit or resize budget, but images exceeding the post-processing patch limit are rejected rather than automatically reduced.

**References**: [Images and vision › Choose an image detail level](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/images-vision) · [Images and vision › Image input requirements](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/images-vision)

questions.title: Review an evaluation plan before migrating to Sonnet 5.5
questions.prompt:
A Claude API customer-inquiry summarization team compares Sonnet 4.6 and Sonnet 5.5 on the same 400-item evaluation set. Conditions:

- Current Sonnet 4.6 requests omit the `thinking` field and use `temperature: 0` and `max_tokens: 600`. Summaries are about 400 tokens.
- The grading script reads `content[0].text`.
- This is an **interactive feature** with support staff waiting on-screen, so the comparison includes accuracy and **p95 latency**.
- Sonnet 5.5 is measured with **the actual intended production settings**. Thinking is not displayed.

Mark each planned statement Yes if supported by the documentation and conditions, otherwise No.

1. Remove temperature for Sonnet 5.5, evaluate medium or low effort for the interactive feature, and record the effort in the comparison.
2. Use `thinking: {"type": "between_tools"}` to avoid initial thinking latency, and raise effort to xhigh to offset quality loss.
3. Leaving display at its default means no thinking block is returned because it is not shown, so the grading script needs no change.
4. `max_tokens: 600` applies only to summary text, so if summary length is similar to Sonnet 4.6, truncation risk is unchanged.

items.text: Remove temperature for Sonnet 5.5, evaluate medium or low effort for the interactive feature, and record the effort in the comparison.
Use thinking type between_tools to avoid initial thinking latency, and raise effort to xhigh to offset quality loss.
Leaving display at its default means no thinking block is returned because it is not shown, so the grading script needs no change.
max_tokens 600 applies only to summary text, so if summary length is similar to Sonnet 4.6, truncation risk is unchanged.

questions.explanation:
The decisive facts are interactive use and p95 latency, production settings, content[0].text, and a `max_tokens: 600` cap for approximately 400-token summaries. Each statement combines at least two migration-guide facts with these conditions. Claude evaluation guidance recommends including dimensions such as latency and using the same evaluation set as the baseline.

- **1 (Yes)**: Nondefault temperature causes a 400 on Sonnet 5.5 and must be removed. Default API effort is high; latency-sensitive chat should start at medium or low. There is no fixed mapping to older thinking budgets, so the guide recommends evaluating two or three effort levels and recording the chosen value.
- **2 (No)**: between_tools does disable initial thinking, but is accepted only with low, medium, or high effort. xhigh and max cause 400 errors, preventing evaluation.
- **3 (No)**: Default `display` is `"omitted"`, but thinking blocks still arrive with empty thinking fields and signatures. A response may start with such a block, breaking content[0].text. Find blocks by type before comparison.
- **4 (No)**: max_tokens covers both thinking and text, and thinking is billed as output. The same text also uses roughly 30% more tokens than Sonnet 4.6, depending on content, so a previously 400-token summary approaches 600 by itself. Recount tokens and reassess limits and cost.

Also note: `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` causes a 400 on Sonnet 5.5; between_tools is the lowest-thinking setting. Cost comparisons must use Sonnet 5.5 response usage, not old Sonnet 4.6 counts.

**References**: [Sonnet 5.5 migration guide › Migrating to Claude Sonnet 5.5 from Claude Sonnet 4.6 and earlier Sonnet models](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/sonnet-5-5/migration-guide) · [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Define your success criteria](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

questions.title: Grade weekly evaluations combining format and tone
questions.prompt:
A customer-response generation team evaluates about 3,000 answers weekly against two success criteria:

- The first line must contain a ticket number: "TCK-" followed by six digits.
- The tone must be empathetic.

Grading constraints:

- Ticket-number judgments must be **identical on every rerun**.
- Tone must be scored for **every response each week**, supporting **numeric weekly trends**.
- Human reviewers have only **three hours per week, about 100 responses**.
- The proposed tone-grading model's **reliability has never been verified**.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Use a regex for ticket numbers; use a model different from the generator with a rubric and 1–5 tone scale, first checking agreement against 100 human ratings.
Use a single model different from the generator to grade both criteria with a rubric and 1–5 scale; humans co-grade 100 each week to check agreement.
Use a regex for ticket numbers; humans score a random 100 responses for tone on a 1–5 scale to estimate trends across all 3,000.
Use a regex for ticket numbers; immediately score all tone responses with a different model and a 1–5 rubric, while humans rewrite low-scoring answers.

questions.explanation:
Each constraint excludes a distractor. Claude evaluation guidance recommends the fastest, most reliable, scalable grading method. Code-based exact or string matching is fastest and most reliable. Model grading suits complex judgments but should be validated before scaling. Humans offer the highest quality but are slow and expensive, so avoid relying on them where possible. Model grading should use detailed rubrics, concrete scales such as 1–5, and a different model from the generator. {{option:A}} spends scarce human time validating the grader while satisfying all four constraints.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Code makes format judgments reproducible; model grading scores all tone outputs numerically; humans establish reliability.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Tone and reliability checks are appropriate, but model grading of deterministic format cannot guarantee identical reruns.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It fits human capacity but scores only 100, violating all-response scoring and relying on a small manual sample rather than large-scale automated grading.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: It scores everything but deploys an unvalidated grader, contrary to reliability-first guidance and the fourth condition.

Also note: Documentation says enabling thinking and reasoning before assigning scores can improve model grading on complex judgments.

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Grade your evaluations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests) · [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Tips for LLM-based grading](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests) · [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Build evaluations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

questions.title: Which method meets Requirement 1?
questions.context:
> **[Company overview]** Onsaemi Retail is an online household-goods store. Its support chatbot and review analysis use Gemini Interactions API and Gemini 3.8 Flash.
>
> **[Existing environment]** Every chatbot request includes about 60k tokens of shared product policy documents. Prompts currently place the customer question before policy documents. Some developers propose creating explicit cache objects with TTLs. A migration to Gemini 4 Argon is planned next year.
>
> **[Requirement 1]** Reduce chatbot input costs with **minimal code changes**, and verify the effect through response usage information.
>
> **[Requirement 2]** Classify sentiment for about 300,000 reviews each night. Results are needed only by the following afternoon. Total request data is about 600 MB. **Minimize cost.**
>
> **[Operational requirement]** **Duplicate classification distorts statistics**, so a review must not be processed twice. Retry only failed requests.

options.text: Move from Interactions API to generateContent API, create an explicit policy-document cache, and reference it with a specified TTL.
Put policy documents first and customer questions last, then check hits through usage.total_cached_tokens.
Move policies into File Search and retrieve only relevant passages for each question to reduce input tokens.
Keep the order but shorten customer questions, then inspect usage to measure token reduction.

questions.explanation:
The decisive facts are the current question-before-policy order and Requirement 1's minimal code change and usage verification. Gemini 2.5 and later enable implicit caching by default, automatically applying savings on hits. Documentation recommends putting large shared content first and sending similar prefixes close together. The question currently changes the prefix every time; reordering fixes this. The 60k-token context exceeds Gemini 3.8 Flash's 4,096-token minimum.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: The explicit-cache suggestion is a distractor. Interactions API does not support explicit caching; supported Gemini 3 and 2.5 models require generateContent, a substantial migration. Gemini 4 Argon and later do not support explicit caching either, conflicting with next year's plan.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Reordering activates implicit-cache opportunities and usage fields verify the effect.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Retrieval can reduce input but requires a new architecture, exceeding minimal change.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: The change is small, but the dominant 60k-token policy remains, and the varying question prefix still prevents cache hits.

**References**: [Context caching › Implicit caching](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching) · [Context caching › Explicit caching](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching)

questions.title: Which processing method meets Requirement 2 and the operational requirement?
questions.context:
> **[Company overview]** Onsaemi Retail is an online household-goods store. Its support chatbot and review analysis use Gemini Interactions API and Gemini 3.8 Flash.
>
> **[Existing environment]** Every chatbot request includes about 60k tokens of shared product policy documents. Prompts currently place the customer question before policy documents. Some developers propose creating explicit cache objects with TTLs. A migration to Gemini 4 Argon is planned next year.
>
> **[Requirement 1]** Reduce chatbot input costs with **minimal code changes**, and verify the effect through response usage information.
>
> **[Requirement 2]** Classify sentiment for about 300,000 reviews each night. Results are needed only by the following afternoon. Total request data is about 600 MB. **Minimize cost.**
>
> **[Operational requirement]** **Duplicate classification distorts statistics**, so a review must not be processed twice. Retry only failed requests.

options.text: Put all 300,000 requests inline in batch creation, assigning metadata.key per request to match results to review IDs.
Send maximum concurrent standard API requests overnight, use exponential backoff on 429s, and record processed review IDs.
Create a batch from JSONL; if it remains unfinished for hours, create another from the same file and use whichever finishes first.
Upload JSONL through File API, create the batch, then use failedRequestCount and key to resubmit only failures after completion.

questions.explanation:
The decisive facts are next-afternoon results, about 600 MB, minimum cost, no duplicate classification, and failure-only retries. Gemini Batch API costs 50% of standard processing with a target turnaround of 24 hours. Inline requests suit totals below 20 MB; larger batches should use JSONL input files up to 2 GB.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: Keys correctly match results, but 600 MB greatly exceeds the under-20-MB inline range.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for another situation)**: Recording IDs can prevent duplicates, but a large nonurgent workload misses batch discounts, violating minimum cost.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: violates a constraint)**: File input and discounts are right, but batch creation is not idempotent. Repeating a creation request produces a separate job and processes reviews twice.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It combines large-file input and discounts, checks batchStats.failedRequestCount and per-line errors after completion, and uses matching keys to resubmit only failed requests.

Also note: Batches pending or running for over 48 hours expire without results; then resubmit or divide into smaller batches.

**References**: [Batch API › Input file](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-api) · [Batch API › Best practices](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-api)

questions.title: When instructions forbidding Markdown do not work
questions.prompt:
An API summarizes internal reports. Its system prompt says, “Do not use Markdown. Do not use bullets or bold text.” List markers still occasionally appear and render poorly. The developer must:

- Change **prompt wording only**, not request parameters, call structure, or model.
- Add **no output postprocessing code**.
- Follow provider guidance by **describing the desired result**.

Which revision is most appropriate?

options.text: Strengthen the prohibition to “Never use Markdown under any circumstances.”
Lower temperature to reduce variation while leaving the prompt unchanged.
Request smoothly flowing prose paragraphs and remove Markdown formatting from the system prompt itself.
Add a regular-expression filter to remove list markers while leaving the prompt unchanged.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are prompt-wording-only changes and describing the desired result. Claude recommends stating what output should look like rather than listing prohibitions, giving smoothly flowing prose paragraphs as an alternative to “Do not use Markdown.” It also notes that reducing Markdown in the prompt itself may reduce it in outputs.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It changes only text and adds no postprocessing, but strengthens a prohibition rather than describing the desired result.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It changes a request parameter and leaves the formatting instruction issue unresolved.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It describes the desired output and aligns prompt style using wording changes alone.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It can hide rendering problems but adds prohibited postprocessing.

The documentation also presents placing prose within tags such as <smoothly_flowing_prose_paragraphs> as a formatting-control technique.

**References**: [Claude Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: A chatbot follows a user’s “ignore the previous rules” message
questions.prompt:
A customer-support chatbot has application rules defining prohibited topics and answer format. A user’s “Ignore all previous rules” message disrupts compliance. Currently, rules are prepended to the user message on every request. The developer wants to place rules in an instruction layer that:

- Has **higher priority than user input**.
- Does **not repeat rules after user input**.
- Uses a role **distinct from model-generated responses** in history.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep rules at the start of the user message and repeat them after the user input.
Prepend the rules as an assistant message to make them look like prior model agreement.
Move rules into a separate user message immediately before the user input, with nothing appended afterward.
Put rules in a developer message or system_instruction, and send user input as a separate user message.

questions.explanation:
Higher instruction priority and a role distinct from generated responses are decisive. OpenAI describes developer messages as application rules and business logic that take precedence over user messages, while assistant messages represent model-generated responses. Gemini similarly uses system_instruction to configure behavior. Application rules belong in that developer-authority layer, separate from user input.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Rules remain at user priority, and repeating them afterward also violates the constraint.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: approach for a different situation)**: The assistant role represents generated responses, not application rules. It suits prior response examples and violates the required role distinction.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Separate messages still share user priority, so the rules are not higher priority.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Developer-authority rules and user-layer input have distinct roles and priorities.

OpenAI’s instructions parameter applies only to the current request. When using previous_response_id, prior-turn instructions do not remain in context and must be sent again each request.

**References**: [OpenAI Prompt engineering](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering) · [Gemini Text generation](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/text-generation)

questions.title: JSON key changes after a model update
questions.prompt:
An order-analysis service suffers parsing failures when response JSON key names change immediately after a provider model update. It uses an alias model ID that can point to different versions over time. The team already has an evaluation set of input/expected-output pairs. Prevention must:

- Keep **production responses unchanged without team approval**, even when the provider releases a version.
- Switch only **after the new version passes evaluations**.
- Limit changes to **model selection and deployment procedures**, without new service logic.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Pin a dated model snapshot ID and promote new snapshots only after they pass the evaluation set.
Keep the alias, evaluate it daily, and alert and roll back settings when scores drop.
Pin a snapshot and promote new snapshots after a staff member reads a few sample responses.
Pin a snapshot and gate upgrades on evaluations, but also add a service translation layer normalizing version-specific key names.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are no unapproved production changes and evaluation-gated upgrades. OpenAI recommends pinning production to specific snapshots for consistent behavior and measuring prompt or model-version changes with evaluations. With an existing evaluation set, pinning and gated promotion satisfy both.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It stabilizes production through model selection and deployment changes alone, with evaluations gating promotion.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Evaluation detects trouble only after the alias changes and production behavior has already changed without approval.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Pinning helps, but reading a few samples is not passing the required evaluation set.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: It meets stability and evaluation requirements but adds service logic outside the allowed scope. An evaluation gate already prevents a key-changing version reaching production.

**References**: [OpenAI Prompt engineering](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering) · [Claude Choosing a model](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/choosing-a-model)

questions.title: Using irrelevant evidence from a long bundle of minutes
questions.prompt:
An internal tool using Claude Sonnet 5.5 answers factual questions from about 65k tokens of meeting minutes. Minutes are wrapped in <document> tags near the top and the question is last, but answers frequently cite unrelated meetings. The prompt revision must:

- Use one request with **no additional API calls**.
- Add **no infrastructure**, such as search.
- Show the **original supporting passages** with the answer for user comparison.
- A small latency increase is acceptable.

Which revision is most appropriate?

options.text: Add meeting title and date in <source> tags within each <document> and request those metadata at the answer’s end.
Ask the model to first extract verbatim passages relevant to the question and include those quotations with its answer.
Use a first request to summarize each meeting and a second request to answer from summaries, showing summary passages as evidence.
Chunk minutes into a vector index and retrieve top passages for each prompt, displaying them as evidence.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are no extra calls, no new infrastructure, and visible original passages. Claude recommends quoting relevant passages first in long-document tasks to focus attention on relevant material. Document and source metadata tags also help structure multiple documents, but merely strengthen the existing structure without exposing supporting passages.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It adds neither calls nor infrastructure and identifies meetings, but does not show original supporting passages for comparison.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Relevant extraction within one request reduces unrelated grounding and preserves quotations in the response. The small latency cost is allowed.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Summarization can lose detail and, decisively, adds a prohibited API call.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Retrieval can reduce input and show passages but introduces an index and search infrastructure.

**References**: [Claude Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Matching output symptoms to corrective actions
questions.prompt: A customer-inquiry classification team reports five output-quality problems. Match each symptom to the most direct corrective action. One of the six actions is unused.

options.text: Declare the required output structure through a schema.
Add instructions specifying response length and organization.
Repeatedly measure before-and-after results on a fixed set of cases.
Make demonstration answers follow consistent notation conventions.
Specify the response-style standard in system instructions.
Run the same prompt on a larger model.

items.text: Four demonstration answers in the prompt use inconsistent labels and delimiters, and outputs mix formats and labels across calls.
The same inquiry receives polite language in some calls and casual language in others; the prompt says nothing about tone.
Required JSON fields are missing or keys are misspelled, occasionally breaking the receiving parser.
Long greetings and background explanations surround the single needed line, cluttering the interface.
After prompt changes, teammates decide whether to deploy based only on a feeling that results seem better.

questions.explanation:
Each symptom points to a different cause. All five targeted methods work for their matching problem; changing models directly addresses none of these causes.

| Symptom | Action | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | {{option:d}}: Standardize demonstrations | Gemini recommends consistent structure and formatting across few-shot examples. Inconsistent examples lead to mixed outputs. |
| 2 | {{option:e}}: Specify style in system instructions | Tone instructions are missing. Core requirements such as role and persona belong in system instructions or at the prompt’s start. |
| 3 | {{option:a}}: Declare a schema | Missing fields and misspelled keys are structural problems. Structured outputs provide parseable schema-conforming output. |
| 4 | {{option:b}}: Specify length and organization | Extra material reflects unspecified scope and length. OpenAI latency guidance also recommends requesting concision. |
| 5 | {{option:c}}: Repeatedly evaluate fixed cases | The issue is measuring change impact. Claude emphasizes use-case-specific evaluations. |
| Unused | {{option:f}}: Change models | These are prompt, structure, and measurement problems. Evaluation and prompt improvements come first. |

**References**: [Gemini Prompt design strategies](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Claude Structured outputs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs) · [OpenAI Latency optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization) · [Claude Choosing a model](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/choosing-a-model)

questions.title: Evaluating prompt structure and settings
questions.prompt: Mark each statement Yes or No according to the platforms’ official documentation.

items.text: A Claude Sonnet 5.5 service prefills the final assistant message with { to force JSON; the request succeeds and the model continues generating JSON after it.
An OpenAI developer message arranged as identity, instructions, examples, and context, with request-specific customer information near the end, keeps the fixed prefix identical across requests.
For a Gemini request querying 200,000 tokens of documents, guidance recommends documents first and the specific question at the end.
A temperature value of 0.2 in a Gemini 3.6 Flash request is ignored, and a deprecation-warning header asks that it be removed from request settings.

questions.explanation:
1. **No**: Claude documentation says models from 4.6 onward do not support prefilling the final assistant turn; such requests return a 400 error. This older technique is no longer a formatting-control option. Assistant messages earlier in the conversation are unaffected.
2. **Yes**: OpenAI describes a typical developer-message structure of identity, instructions, examples, then context. Variable context belongs near the end. Caching guidance also puts static content first and variable content last, preserving a common prefix across requests.
3. **Yes**: Gemini recommends providing context first and placing specific questions or instructions at the end, using a bridge such as “Based on the information above.”
4. **Yes**: Gemini documentation says Gemini 4 and models from 3.6 onward ignore user values for temperature, top_p, and top_k and return warning headers, so these should be removed from request settings.

**References**: [Claude Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [OpenAI Prompt engineering](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering) · [OpenAI Prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) · [Gemini Long context](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/long-context) · [Gemini Text generation](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/text-generation)

questions.title: Some of twelve instructions are skipped
questions.prompt:
One product-review prompt contains 12 instructions, including language detection, summarization, sentiment classification, personal-data masking, tone, and JSON format. The model sometimes omits masking and formatting. Two examples demonstrate the desired output format. Select TWO improvements subject to:

- At most **three calls per review** are allowed.
- **Total input tokens must not increase substantially**.
- **Model and request parameters stay unchanged**.
- Preserve the examples’ **output format**.

options.text: Repeat masking and format instructions three times each, nearly doubling prompt length.
Group instructions by purpose into two or three prompts, chaining each output into the next input.
Lower temperature to 0 to improve compliance with all twelve instructions.
Move essential constraints such as role and output format into system instructions or to the prompt’s beginning, placing remaining instructions afterward.
Remove both examples to shorten the prompt and focus the model on instructions alone.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints permit up to three calls while preserving token volume, model, and parameters. Gemini recommends decomposing complex prompts into simpler components and chaining sequential tasks so one output feeds the next. It also recommends putting core behavioral constraints, role, and format requirements in system instructions or at the start of the user prompt. Neither approach requires large token growth or parameter changes.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Repetition aims to emphasize missed rules but nearly doubles input, violating the token constraint.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It reduces instructions per call, at the allowed cost of up to three calls.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It changes a parameter. Gemini 3.6 onward and Gemini 4 also ignore temperature, so benefit is unlikely.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It moves essential role and format requirements to the earliest instruction position.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It reduces tokens but removes the format demonstrations, risking violation of the preserved-format requirement.

**References**: [Gemini Prompt design strategies](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Gemini Text generation](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/text-generation)

questions.title: Constructing a request comparing two screenshots
questions.prompt:
A Claude API feature compares UI screenshots before and after a change. The initial content must:

- Send both at **original resolution**, without compositing or downscaling.
- Follow the recommended **images first, text afterward** layout.
- Introduce each image with a **text label usable in follow-up references**.

Which layout is most appropriate?

options.text: Put the comparison question first, followed by each image preceded by “Image 1:” or “Image 2:”.
Combine both screenshots horizontally into one image first, then refer to the left and right screens.
Put both images first without labels, then ask the question using “first image” and “second image.”
Place “Image 1:” and the first image, then “Image 2:” and the second image, followed by the comparison question.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are image-first placement and named labels. Claude documentation says images work best before text. For multiple images, short introductory labels such as “Image 1:” and “Image 2:” support references in the prompt and later turns. Multiple images can be analyzed in one request.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Labels exist, but the question precedes images. Text-first or interleaved layouts can work, but guidance prefers text after images where possible.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Compositing changes how original images are delivered and may reduce them to fit one image’s size limit.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Order is correct, but no introductory text labels support later named references such as “Image 1.”
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Original images appear first with labels, followed by the question.

**References**: [Claude Vision](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision)

questions.title: Three sequential questions about the same site photo
questions.prompt:
A Gemini API site-inspection app asks three sequential questions about one uploaded 8MB photo: identify hazards, use that result to ask hazard coordinates, then draft a report using both results. Requirements:

- Do **not retransmit photo data for every request**.
- Follow Gemini’s single-image guidance to place the **text prompt before the image**.
- Questions depend on preceding results and **cannot be combined into one request**.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Include the photo as inline base64 in all three requests, with text before the image.
Upload once through Files API and reuse its URI in all three requests, with image before text.
Upload once through Files API and reuse its URI in all three requests, with text before the image.
Upload once through Files API and combine all three questions into one request.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are avoiding retransmission and text-first placement. Gemini says inline image data counts toward the total 20MB request limit, including prompts and system instructions. Files API is recommended for large files or images reused across requests. For one image plus text, the text prompt should precede the image in the input array.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Placement is correct, but it retransmits the 8MB photo three times.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: File reuse is correct, but image-first order contradicts the single-image guidance.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It reuses one uploaded file and follows the placement guidance.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It avoids retransmission but combines questions that depend on earlier results, violating the sequential-call requirement.

**References**: [Gemini Image understanding](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/image-understanding)

questions.title: Unstable readings of tiny gauge markings
questions.prompt:
A Gemini 3-family model reads small gauge values in equipment photos, but readings vary across calls for the same photo. The team **prioritizes accuracy**. Select TWO improvements subject to:

- Keep the model unchanged.
- Accept a **small increase in tokens and latency per image**, but no extra calls.
- Do **not reduce detail in gauge markings**.

options.text: Lower thinking_level to reduce reasoning tokens and latency, then test readings at that setting.
