Increase media_resolution to raise the maximum tokens allocated per image.
Call three times per photo, choose the most common value, and ask a person if all differ.
Halve image dimensions before upload to reduce transfer time and cost.
Check and correct image rotation and blur first.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements prioritize accuracy, prohibit extra calls, and preserve detail. Gemini’s media_resolution, introduced with Gemini 3, sets the maximum tokens allocated per input image or video frame. Higher values help with small text and details but increase tokens and latency. Documentation also recommends correctly rotated, sharp, unblurred images.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: thinking_level controls reasoning, not image-token allocation, and reduces reasoning despite the accuracy priority.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It directly increases usable image information at the permitted token and latency cost.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Voting may reduce variability, but triples calls, violating both limited overhead and no-extra-call requirements. It does not improve the input’s readability.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Transfer improves but gauge detail is reduced.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Tilted or blurred inputs remain hard to read even at higher resolution. Correcting input improves reading conditions without added model cost.

**References**: [Gemini Image understanding](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/image-understanding)

questions.title: Responding to retirement of stored prompt objects
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI API team has managed prompts through provider-hosted prompt objects with IDs and versions. It receives notice that this feature will retire. Future prompt changes must:

- **Not depend on the retiring feature**.
- Have history that can be **code-reviewed and rolled back**.
- Support **reproducible before-and-after comparisons on identical evaluation inputs**.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue using stored prompt objects and increment dashboard versions to compare responses.
Version prompt text in the repository and compare revisions using the same evaluation set.
Keep prompt text where it is and document dated change history in dashboard notes and a wiki.
Edit production prompts directly and restore previous wording if problems appear.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are independence from the retiring feature, reviewable rollback, and reproducible evaluation. OpenAI recommends keeping production prompts in application code instead of reusable prompt objects, which are being retired, and measuring prompt or model changes with evaluations.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Comparison remains possible but depends on the retiring feature.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Repository versions support review and rollback, while the same evaluation set enables reproducible comparisons.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Notes and wiki history are not code review and may diverge from executed text, making rollback and reproduction difficult.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is simple but leaves no reliable basis for rerunning the previous prompt on identical inputs.

**References**: [OpenAI Prompt engineering](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering)

questions.title: Responses remain long after lowering effort
questions.prompt:
A Claude Opus 5 report-summary service receives complaints about long answers. Long system instructions and documents are cached while a conversation receives repeated questions. Testing effort at low did not noticeably shorten responses. The final change must:

- **Maintain current summary quality**.
- **Preserve prompt-cache hits**, avoiding reprocessing cached prefixes.
- Avoid **truncated responses**.
- Keep the **same model**.

Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep effort at its default and explicitly request summary length and structure, such as at most three key paragraphs.
Operate with effort low, accepting unchanged length and only taking cost savings.
Reduce max_tokens to force the response to stop at a fixed length.
Use a smaller Sonnet-family model to obtain shorter answers.

questions.explanation:
Cache preservation, quality, and no truncation are decisive. Claude documentation says changing Opus 5 effort does not reliably change visible answer length; length should be requested explicitly in the prompt. Changing top-level effort between requests also invalidates previous-turn cached prefixes, so effort should remain stable in cached conversations.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Direct length instructions address the cause, while unchanged effort preserves the cache.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Effort does not solve length, lower effort may reduce capability and quality, and changing it requires reprocessing the cached prefix.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: max_tokens is a hard ceiling and may truncate the summary mid-sentence.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It changes the prohibited model and also requires a new cache.

**References**: [Claude Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices) · [Claude Effort](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort)

questions.title: A classification prompt copies twelve examples
questions.prompt:
A prompt classifying customer inquiries into eight categories contains 12 few-shot examples. The model copies example wording even for new input and misclassifies inquiry types absent from the examples. Select TWO fixes subject to:

- Change **prompt text only**, not request parameters.
- Keep the **current model**.
- **Do not increase input tokens**.

options.text: Remove similar examples, retaining only the most relevant 3–5.
Increase temperature to encourage departures from example wording.
Select retained examples to represent diverse inquiry types and edge cases.
Increase to 24 examples, using three per category.
Run the same prompt on a larger model to reduce example overfitting.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are no token increase and prompt-text-only changes. Gemini warns that excessive examples can cause overfitting. Claude recommends 3–5 examples closely reflecting real use, including edge cases, with enough diversity to avoid teaching unintended patterns.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It reduces redundant examples and the source of overfitting while reducing tokens.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It changes a forbidden parameter and leaves example composition unchanged.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Diverse representative examples improve generalization to types not explicitly shown.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: More types may be covered, but 24 examples substantially increase tokens and overfitting risk.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It changes the model and leaves the example-design cause unchanged.

**References**: [Gemini Prompt design strategies](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies) · [Claude Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)

questions.title: Parsing still fails despite “JSON only” instructions
questions.prompt: A feature extracts fields from order notes. Despite “Output JSON only,” occasional surrounding prose or missing keys breaks parsing. All three providers offer JSON-schema structured outputs. The team wants the **most reliable way to eliminate parsing failures**. Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Add three more correct JSON examples to the prompt.
Extract JSON with a regular expression and fill missing keys with default values.
Retry the same request automatically up to three times after parsing failure.
Enable structured outputs with the extraction result’s JSON schema in the request.

questions.explanation:
The key criterion is reliability. Claude explains that constrained decoding produces parseable schema-conforming outputs, avoiding retries for schema violations, while even careful prompting can produce invalid JSON or missing required fields. Gemini likewise says structured outputs guarantee syntactically valid JSON.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: confusion between techniques)**: Examples improve consistency but do not constrain generation to a schema, leaving failure risk.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: It hides symptoms afterward, and default-filled missing keys may pass incorrect data as valid.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It reduces but does not eliminate failure probability and adds latency and cost, falling short of the most reliable approach.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It enforces output structure at generation, addressing the cause.

Claude separately documents exceptions such as refusal and reaching max_tokens, where output may not match the schema. Inspect stop_reason before parsing.

**References**: [Claude Structured outputs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs) · [OpenAI Structured outputs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs) · [Gemini Structured output](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/structured-output)

questions.title: Required fields are missing in JSON mode
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI Responses API feature extracts contract parties and amounts. It uses json_object in text.format (JSON mode), producing valid JSON but occasionally missing required fields. The change must:

- **Guarantee schema adherence**.
- **Keep Responses API**, without changing endpoints.
- Add **no calls due to parsing failures**.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep json_object and describe required fields and types in greater detail in the prompt.
Change text.format to json_schema and supply strict: true and field definitions.
Move to Chat Completions while retaining json_object in response_format.
Keep json_object and request another response whenever fields are missing.

questions.explanation:
Schema adherence, the same endpoint, and no extra calls are decisive. OpenAI says JSON mode guarantees valid JSON but not schema adherence. Structured Outputs uses json_schema with strict: true to enforce the schema and is preferred where available. Responses API configures it through text.format.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Detailed prompting helps but JSON mode still cannot guarantee the schema.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It switches to a schema-guaranteeing format within Responses API, meeting all three constraints.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It changes endpoints while retaining the same JSON-mode omission problem.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It adds calls after detecting omissions and still offers no schema guarantee.

json_schema is supported by models from gpt-4o-2024-08-06 onward. Safety refusals can still be detected programmatically with structured outputs.

**References**: [OpenAI Structured outputs](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs)

questions.title: Schema-valid outputs contain implausible values
questions.prompt:
A Gemini structured-output feature extracts invoice-image fields. Responses always pass schema validation, but due_date sometimes contains an absent value such as “2099-01-01.” Downstream systems depend on the current schema. Requirements:

- Keep the **model and schema structure unchanged**.
- Reject invalid dates **before DB storage**.
- Allow **at most one retry per case**.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Validate date ranges in the app before storage, regenerate once if invalid, and send persistent failures to a review queue.
Split due_date into integer year, month, and day fields with permitted ranges.
Store schema-valid responses unchanged and have staff repair unusual dates in a month-end batch.
Validate before storage and regenerate up to five times until the value passes.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints preserve schema structure, require pre-storage rejection, and limit retries to one. Gemini says structured output guarantees syntactically valid JSON, but values may be semantically wrong; applications must validate values and handle errors. It also recommends helpful description fields and strong types such as enums.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: The app performs semantic validation, retries once, and routes unresolved cases to people without storing them.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Strong typing is recommended, but splitting fields changes the downstream schema contract.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Repair occurs only after invalid data is stored.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Validation precedes storage, but five retries exceed the one-retry limit.

**References**: [Gemini Structured output](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/structured-output)

questions.title: Chunk parsing errors in streamed structured output
questions.prompt:
A Gemini structured-output stream should show partial results, but parsing each chunk as JSON almost always fails. Requirements:

- Preserve the perceived-latency goal of showing **first characters and partial results** while waiting.
- **Validate the final object against the schema** before saving.
- Complete with **one structured-output request**.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Disable streaming and parse the completed response all at once.
Accumulate chunks and display them with a partial JSON parser, then save the last parsed result without validation.
Accumulate chunks for partial JSON display, then parse the complete response and validate its schema when the stream ends.
Stream free text without structured output and convert it to JSON in a second request.

questions.explanation:
Partial display, final validation, and one request are decisive. Gemini says each streamed chunk is a partial JSON string; concatenation forms the final object. Individual chunks are not complete JSON and fail standalone parsing. Documentation also requires application validation because values may be semantically wrong.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Parsing errors disappear, but nothing is displayed until completion, abandoning partial display.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Partial display works, but final schema validation is omitted and incorrect values may be saved.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It accumulates for partial display, then fully parses and validates. The tradeoff is adding a partial JSON parser.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Free-text streaming works but conversion requires a prohibited second request.

**References**: [Gemini Structured output](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/structured-output)

questions.title: A document-summary screen feels frozen
questions.prompt:
After users click summarize, a screen remains unchanged for several seconds and feels frozen. Documents differ per request and the system prompt is short. The team wants the **largest reduction in perceived waiting** while:

- Keeping **summary quality and the current model**.
- Limiting changes to **response handling**.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Halve the system instructions to reduce input tokens.
Use a smaller model for faster generation.
Enable streaming and display text as it is generated.
Cache the system-prompt prefix to reduce repeated processing.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are the largest perceived improvement and response-handling-only changes. OpenAI identifies streaming as the most effective way to reduce user waiting. It notes that halving input tokens may improve latency by only 1–5%. Claude explains that stream: true delivers server-sent events as generation proceeds.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: confusion between optimizations)**: The effect may be small, and an already short prompt offers little reduction.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It may be faster but violates the model and quality requirements.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Even if total generation time is unchanged, early visible content greatly reduces perceived waiting, with changes confined to response handling.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: approach for a different situation)**: Caching benefits long repeated prefixes. Short instructions and changing documents offer little reusable content.

**References**: [OpenAI Latency optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization) · [Claude Streaming](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/streaming)

questions.title: Intermittent OpenAI API 429 errors
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI document-classification service intermittently receives rate-limit 429 errors, unrelated to billing or quota. Outputs are about one label line, but max_tokens is 4,000. Some responses include Retry-After. Constraints:

- Keep **real-time responses**, model, prompt, and output format unchanged.
- Avoid inflating the **per-request token estimate** used for limits.
- Failed requests also count, so **retries must not worsen limit pressure**.

Select TWO documented responses.

options.text: Immediately repeat every 429 request without delay until successful.
Reduce max_tokens to a level appropriate for one label line.
Wait at least Retry-After when present, add random jitter, and cap attempts and total retry time.
Batch several classifications into one call by redesigning the prompt and output format.
Raise every request’s max_tokens to the model maximum to prevent truncation.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements avoid inflated estimates and retry storms. OpenAI says rate-limit accounting uses the larger of max_tokens and the estimated token count based on character count, recommending max_tokens near expected response size. Retries should use exponential backoff and jitter, treat Retry-After as a minimum wait, and cap attempts and elapsed retry time.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Failed requests count toward per-minute limits. Immediate repetition increases pressure and does not resolve it.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Aligning the estimate with actual output allows more requests within the same limit.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It respects server waiting guidance and uses jitter and caps to prevent retry storms.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It may reduce calls but changes the prohibited prompt and output format.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Larger max_tokens inflates rate-limit estimates and can increase 429 frequency.

**References**: [OpenAI Rate limits](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/rate-limits)

questions.title: Gemini 429 errors persist after splitting API keys
questions.prompt:
A Gemini app runs daytime interactive requests and tens of thousands of overnight document summaries in one project. Frequent 429s persist after distributing requests across three API keys. Requirements:

- Resolve this week **without new projects or extra payment**.
- Bulk summaries need finish **by the next morning**, not immediately.
- Daytime interactive requests remain **real time**.

Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Move overnight bulk work to Batch API with its separate limits and apply backoff to interactive requests.
Increase to five keys with round-robin distribution in the same project and apply interactive backoff.
Move overnight work to a separate Google Cloud project and apply interactive backoff.
Reduce overnight volume until a higher tier becomes available and also lower interactive call frequency.

questions.explanation:
No new projects or payment and the next-morning deadline are decisive. Gemini limits apply per project, not per API key, so extra keys do not increase capacity. Batch requests have separate limits from standard calls; moving nonurgent overnight work reduces pressure on interactive limits.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It isolates nonurgent load under separate limits and applies backoff to real-time requests. The tradeoff is deferred batch processing.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Project-level limits do not increase with key count; it repeats the already ineffective approach.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: A separate project genuinely separates limits, but violates the no-new-project condition.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Automatic tier upgrades depend on payment history and elapsed time, conflicting with resolution this week without extra payment. Throttling interactive work also conflicts with real-time service.

Requests-per-day limits reset at midnight Pacific Time.

**References**: [Gemini Rate limits](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits)

questions.title: Branching on overnight pipeline 429 errors
questions.prompt:
An unattended overnight document pipeline calls Claude and OpenAI APIs. It begins receiving 429s without retry-after headers, but response bodies identify the error type. Causes may be transient rate limits or exhausted spending limits or quota. Requirements:

- **Immediately notify staff** when recovery needs human action.
- Do **not keep retrying exhausted limits**.
- **Automatically recover** from transient rate-limit 429s.
- Use **only the two approved providers**.

Which handling is most appropriate?

options.text: Retry every 429 up to eight times with exponential backoff and jitter, then record failure and continue.
Classify the response body; stop and notify without retrying spending-limit or quota exhaustion, and use capped backoff for other rate limits.
Stop and notify staff for every 429 regardless of type, awaiting manual resumption.
Automatically switch to an unapproved provider if 429s repeat.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements prohibit retrying exhausted limits while requiring automatic transient recovery. Claude spending-limit 429s lack retry-after and contain error.details.error_code equal to enforced_spend_limit_reached; retries fail until access resumes. For ordinary limits, respect retry-after when present. OpenAI likewise recommends inspecting error bodies and not retrying quota or billing errors requiring intervention.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It may recover transient limits but also retries exhaustion and delays human notification, slowing unattended recovery.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It separates stop-and-notify exhaustion from bounded transient backoff, at the cost of body-parsing logic.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It handles exhaustion but prevents automatic recovery from transient limits.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Work continues but sends data outside approved provider boundaries.

**References**: [Claude Rate limits](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits) · [OpenAI Rate limits](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/rate-limits)

questions.title: Estimating image and PDF input tokens before sending
questions.prompt:
A Claude API feature processes multiple uploaded images and PDFs, currently referenced through Files API file_id. Requests include client tools and a web-search server tool. Pre-request token estimates must:

- Cost **nothing for the estimate call**.
- Use **no message-generation rate-limit capacity**.
- Use the **selected model’s tokenization**.
- Include **image and PDF tokens**.

Select TWO documented methods.

options.text: Convert image and PDF sources to base64 for the count_tokens endpoint.
Send a real generation request with max_tokens set to 1 and read usage.
Implement image-size formulas and average tokens per PDF page in application code.
Estimate inputs without the web-search server tool through count_tokens, then inspect usage on the actual server-tool request.
Count only text with a generic external tokenizer and exclude images and PDFs.

questions.explanation:
Free estimation, independent rate limits, and model-specific tokenization are decisive. Claude token counting is free, has limits independent of message generation, and accepts system prompts, tools, images, and PDFs. Images and PDFs must be base64; url or file sources error. Requests with server tools such as web search or MCP connectors are unsupported for counting, so documentation directs users to the actual response’s usage object.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Replacing file_id references with base64 allows free independent-limit counting including image and PDF tokens.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It yields actual usage but incurs generation cost and consumes message-generation limits.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It includes media but approximates model tokenization and may diverge as models change; image-token limits also differ by generation.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Excluding unsupported server tools from estimation and checking actual usage follows the documented approach.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It excludes required media tokens and differs from Claude tokenization.

Counts are estimates and may differ slightly from actual input usage. Models from Claude 4.7 onward use a new tokenizer that can produce about 30% more tokens for the same text than earlier models.

**References**: [Claude Token counting](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/token-counting)

questions.title: Evaluating reasoning settings
questions.prompt: A backend developer integrating reasoning settings across three platforms is reviewing internal-wiki statements. Judge each against the official documentation.

items.text: Even when a Gemini service returns only thinking summaries, billing uses all generated thinking tokens rather than the amount visible in the summary.
Setting output_config: {"effort": "adaptive"} in Claude lets the model decide whether to think for each request.
A very small max_output_tokens in OpenAI Responses API can be consumed by reasoning before visible output, ending the response as incomplete without visible text.
Calling Gemini 3.8 Flash without thinking settings produces an immediate non-thinking answer, so no thinking tokens are billed.

questions.explanation:
Statements 2 and 4 are incorrect. These independent facts test setting semantics and billing/limit accounting.

1. **Yes**: Gemini bills all thinking tokens the model generates, even if the API returns only a thinking summary. Visible and billed quantities differ.
2. **No**: adaptive is a thinking mode—thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}—not an effort level. Claude warns not to pass adaptive as effort; levels are max, xhigh, high, medium, and low.
3. **Yes**: max_output_tokens includes reasoning, visible output, and formatting tokens. It may be exhausted before visible text, producing incomplete_details.reason of max_output_tokens. OpenAI recommends ample initial headroom.
4. **No**: Thinking is enabled by default in Gemini 3 models; Gemini 3.8 Flash defaults to medium. Omitting settings therefore does not avoid thinking or its charges.

**References**: [Claude Effort › Effort levels](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort) · [OpenAI Reasoning models › Managing the context window](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning) · [Gemini Thinking](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking)

questions.title: Processing a streamed Claude tool call
questions.prompt: A streaming Claude Messages API request includes the client tool get_weather. Arrange the steps from receiving the model’s tool-call decision through returning its result.

items.text: Concatenate tool-input JSON fragments separately for each block.
Execute get_weather in application code.
Append a user message containing tool_result and send the next request.
Send the streaming request and read the tool name and id from the tool-block start event.
When the block-end event arrives, parse the accumulated string as JSON.

questions.explanation:
Tool input arrives as JSON-string fragments rather than a complete object. Each step supplies the next step’s input.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | (4) Start streaming and read name/id at block start | A stream must exist to receive events. | The start event provides id and name, with empty input. |
| 2 | (1) Accumulate input fragments | Fragments arrive after block start and must be grouped by block index. | Fragments are partial_json strings. |
| 3 | (5) Parse after block end | All fragments are needed for complete JSON. | Earlier parsing fails on incomplete JSON. |
| 4 | (2) Execute the tool in the app | Execution requires parsed input. | Client tools run in application code. |
| 5 | (3) Send the next request with tool_result | The result and original id are needed to match tool_use_id. | Preserve the assistant turn unchanged and match IDs. |

Multiple tool calls each have their own block index, so accumulate them separately.

**References**: [Claude Streaming › Streaming tool input](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/streaming) · [Claude Handle tool calls](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls)

questions.title: Separating effort by inquiry type while preserving caching
questions.prompt:
A Claude Sonnet 5.5 support service caches an approximately 12k-token policy prefix with cache_control in each conversation. It handles simple shipping or business-hours questions and complex refund disputes. All currently use default effort. Constraints:

- Preserve **policy-prefix cache hits throughout each conversation**; reprocessing 12k tokens every turn is unacceptable.
- **No beta features** under security policy.
- Simple questions must meet **p95 latency** targets.
- Do **not lower refund-dispute reasoning quality**.

The team accepts an extra classification stage and additional cache-write cost. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Change top-level effort each turn between low for simple questions and high for disputes while using the policy cache.
Classify inquiries at intake into two conversation flows, keep effort fixed throughout each flow, and build a separate policy-prefix cache for each.
Enable the beta that changes effort mid-conversation through output_config in an empty-content system message while preserving the cache.
Fix every conversation at low effort and maintain one policy cache.

questions.explanation:
Cache preservation and the beta prohibition are decisive; latency and dispute quality eliminate one-effort-for-all designs. Claude says changing top-level effort between requests invalidates prompt caching because effort affects the prompt, so previous cache points do not carry forward. A cache-preserving mid-conversation change exists but requires a beta header. Therefore choose effort by type at conversation start and keep it fixed within the conversation.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Per-turn top-level changes invalidate caching and reprocess the 12k-token prefix.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Each flow retains fixed effort and cache continuity. The accepted tradeoffs are classification and separate prefix writes for two effort settings.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Per-message effort preserves prior cache points but requires a forbidden beta header. Sonnet 5.5 support does not change that.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It preserves cache and latency but lowers dispute effort, violating quality requirements.

Five-minute cache writes cost 1.25 times base input, while Sonnet 5.5 reads cost 0.05 times base input. Check whether subsequent read savings offset separate flow writes.

**References**: [Claude Effort › Change effort mid-conversation (beta)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort) · [Claude Prompt caching › What invalidates the cache](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Claude Adaptive thinking › Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/adaptive-thinking)

questions.title: Resuming an advisory conversation after 60 days
questions.prompt:
An insurance-advice app built on OpenAI Responses API must resume a customer’s conversation after as long as 60 days. OpenAI-side response storage is permitted. Requirements:

- Retain **original conversational context after 60 days**.
- Build **no new application history database**.
- Let the model reference **original items**, not summaries.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Store responses with defaults and chain previous_response_id, passing the last response ID when the customer returns.
Store history in an internal database and resend all original items in input when resuming.
Create a Conversations API conversation object at the start and associate all subsequent requests with its conversation ID.
Start a new response chain every 30 days, seeding input with a summary of the previous chain.

questions.explanation:
Original context after 60 days and no new history database are decisive. OpenAI response objects are stored for 30 days by default, so the referenced response may no longer exist after 60 days. Conversations API objects and their items are not subject to the 30-day TTL; items from associated responses are also retained without that TTL.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It is concise to implement but default response expiration violates long-term context. All earlier input tokens in the chain are also billed as input.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Original content is retained but requires a prohibited history store.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: A server-held conversation retains original items without the 30-day expiration.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It avoids expiration but replaces originals with summaries, violating the original-context requirement.

This question does not cover store=false. With response storage disabled, the application must retain and resend items itself.

**References**: [OpenAI Conversation state › Passing context from the previous response](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state) · [OpenAI Conversation state › Using the Conversations API](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state)

questions.title: Adding checks for the latest regulatory changes
questions.prompt:
An internal FAQ app uses a Gemini 3 model through Gemini API and needs a latest-regulation check. New notices appear at new URLs unknown in advance. Requirements:

- **Minimal code changes**, without custom search functions or new server components.
- No **new periodic collection job**, since notices must be available soon after publication.
- Display **source URLs** in answers.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Add the built-in google_search tool to tools and display URLs from url_citation annotations.
Declare a search-service function and implement calls and result parsing, appending result URLs to answers.
Periodically crawl several notice sites and append collected text and site addresses to prompts.
Provide known notice-list page addresses to URL context and display the pages read as sources.

questions.explanation:
Minimal code, no periodic collection, and unknown new notice URLs are decisive. Gemini Google Search grounding is enabled by adding google_search to tools. Response text-block annotations contain url_citation with url, title, and citation-span indices, providing grounding and sources with minimal integration.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: One built-in tool and citation URL display meet all three requirements.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It works but adds custom search integration and parsing outside the minimal-code requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It requires a crawler and schedule, with new notices unavailable until the next collection.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Code is relatively small, but the app must specify URLs in advance, which does not keep up with new notices at unknown addresses.

For Gemini 3 and later, billing counts executed search queries; multiple queries within one request count separately.

**References**: [Gemini Grounding with Google Search › Using the tool](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/google-search) · [Gemini Tools overview](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tools)

questions.title: Function arguments the model should not supply
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI Responses API order app exposes get_order(user_id, order_no). The server already knows user_id from the login session, but the model sometimes fills it with another user number mentioned in conversation. Requirements:

- A **model-supplied user ID must never drive the lookup**, regardless of model accuracy.
- Keep the function’s **body logic unchanged**.
- Maintain **one shared tool definition** for all users, without dynamic user-specific definitions.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Add “Use only the current conversation user’s ID” to the description and enable strict.
Generate a new tool definition per request with an enum containing only the session user ID.
Ignore the provided user_id inside the function body and overwrite it with the session ID.
Remove user_id from the exposed definition, expose only order_no, and have call-handling code inject the session user_id when invoking the existing function.

questions.explanation:
No model-supplied ID, unchanged function body, and one definition are decisive. OpenAI best practices say not to ask the model for arguments code already knows. Removing such values from the definition and injecting them in code eliminates the model’s opportunity to supply an incorrect value. Function results are associated with the call using call_id.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Descriptions and strict constrain shape and intent, not which person’s ID the model chooses, so this still relies on model output.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: A single allowed value can prevent error but changes definitions per request, violating one shared definition.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It ignores model values but changes prohibited function-body logic.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: One definition and the original body remain, while code supplies the trusted session value.

**References**: [OpenAI Function calling › Best practices for defining functions](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling) · [OpenAI Function calling › Handling function calls](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/function-calling)

questions.title: Independent tools are not called in parallel
questions.prompt:
A Claude agent calls three independent lookups sequentially instead of in parallel. Inspection shows that when an assistant turn contains multiple tool_use blocks, each tool_result is inserted as a separate user message. Constraints:

- Keep the **validated model**.
- Do **not edit the approved system prompt**.
- Fix the cause directly in **conversation-history structure**.

Which change is most appropriate?

options.text: Explicitly set disable_parallel_tool_use: false in tool_choice.
Put all three tool_result blocks for one turn’s three tool_use blocks into a single user message.
Add a system instruction to call independent tools simultaneously.
Upgrade to a model that calls tools in parallel more often and keep the same history.

questions.explanation:
The direct history-structure fix is decisive; model and prompt constraints eliminate the other approaches. Claude documents splitting tool_result blocks across separate user messages as the most common cause of reduced parallel tool use. All results belong in one user message.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Parallel use is already allowed by default, so this does not fix history structure.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It applies the documented history format.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Such prompting is a supplementary recommendation when defaults are insufficient, but violates the approved-prompt constraint and leaves the cause.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It changes the model and leaves the history problem.

Within the user message, every tool_result block must precede text. Even skipped calls need a tool_result with is_error: true and a short explanation.

**References**: [Claude Parallel tool use › Message history for parallel tool calls](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use) · [Claude Handle tool calls › Message structure rules](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls)

questions.title: Handling tool failures and reducing invalid inputs
questions.prompt:
A tool wrapping an external API sometimes returns 500 errors, and the model sometimes supplies invalid parameters. Select TWO improvements subject to:

- The model must **recognize failure and choose its next attempt**.
- Do **not expose implementation details**, such as internal paths or stack traces.
- Reduce invalid input through **tool definitions**, not system-prompt wording.

options.text: Return an empty result as a normal response after failures so the model moves on.
Mark failures as errors with a short message explaining what went wrong and what to try next.
Return the full exception stack trace for the model to diagnose.
Enable strict mode in the tool definition to enforce input-schema adherence.
Add “Follow tool parameter formats exactly” to the system prompt and continue.

questions.explanation:
Recognizable failures and definition-level input control are decisive. Claude recommends is_error: true with a message explaining what went wrong and what to try next. strict: true in tool definitions enforces input-schema adherence. The principle applies across all three platforms; these field names are Claude’s.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Without the error marker, the model reads failure as success. Documentation warns that omitting is_error hides errors from the model.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: An explicit error and actionable message let the model choose recovery.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It exposes prohibited implementation details despite revealing failure.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It enforces schema-conforming inputs at the tool-definition level.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Prompt guidance does not guarantee the schema and violates definition-level control.

**References**: [Claude Handle tool calls › Error handling for client tools](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls) · [Claude Tool use overview](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview)

questions.title: Restricting candidate functions for one request
questions.prompt:
A Gemini Interactions API assistant uses the same shared tools declaration of six functions for every request. This refund-processing request must call either lookup_refund or create_refund. Requirements:

- **Require a function call**, not text alone.
- Limit candidates to **those two functions** for this request.
- Keep the shared tools declaration **unchanged across requests**.

Which setting is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep tool_choice at auto and instruct the model to call one of the two functions while retaining all six declarations.
Set tool_choice to any with all six declarations and instruct the model to use only the two functions.
Declare only the two functions in this request’s tools and set tool_choice to any.
Use allowed_tools in tool_choice with mode: any and the two function names, keeping all six declarations.

questions.explanation:
Each requirement eliminates one distractor. Gemini configures calling modes through generation_config.tool_choice: auto is the default, any always predicts a function call, and none disables calls. allowed_tools specifies a mode and tools list, restricting this request’s candidates without changing declarations.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: auto lets the model choose a direct answer, so a call is not guaranteed.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: A call is required but all six remain candidates; prompt wording does not enforce the two-function restriction.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Candidates are restricted but the shared declaration changes.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Request settings enforce both a call and its candidate set without changing declarations.

The documented validated mode guarantees function-schema adherence, but no example combining it with allowed_tools was confirmed, so this question does not use it.

**References**: [Gemini Function calling › Function calling modes](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/function-calling)

questions.title: The OpenAI remote MCP call sequence
questions.prompt: An OpenAI Responses API mcp tool connects to a remote MCP server with user approval required before calls. Arrange the steps from the first request until the response contains the tool result.

items.text: Show the tool name and arguments to the user and obtain a decision.
The API retrieves the MCP server’s tool list and includes it in the response.
Send an item containing approve and the approval request ID in the next request.
The model selects a tool and arguments, proposing a call that appears as an approval request.
The API executes the server tool and returns a call item with arguments and output.

questions.explanation:
OpenAI describes the flow as tool discovery, approval, and execution. Each output supplies the next step.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | (2) Fetch the tool list | Adding the server to tools causes the API to request its list. | A tool-list item appears in the response. |
| 2 | (4) Propose a call and request approval | The model needs the available list to choose a tool. | Approval-required calls appear as approval-request items. |
| 3 | (1) Show the proposal and obtain a decision | The approval item supplies what to display. | Approval precedes sending data to the server. |
| 4 | (3) Send the approval response | The user decision and request ID are required. | The item contains approve and approval_request_id. |
| 5 | (5) Execute remotely and return a call item | Execution waits for the approval response. | The call item contains arguments and output; failures use error. |

Keeping the tool-list item in subsequent context avoids refetching every turn and reduces latency. Each approval applies to only one tool call.

**References**: [OpenAI MCP and Connectors › How it works](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp) · [OpenAI MCP and Connectors › Approvals](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp)

questions.title: Connecting an internal-network-only MCP server
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI Responses API agent must use an inventory MCP server accessible only inside the corporate network. Security policy prohibits public exposure. Requirements:

- Do **not expose the server to the public internet**.
- Make **minimal code changes**, without writing relay integration code.
- Let the model **choose tools and arguments** for each question.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Expose a public HTTPS endpoint with IP restrictions and use it as server_url in the mcp tool.
Have the app prefetch inventory into the prompt so the model answers without selecting tools.
Install a tunnel client internally and specify tunnel_id instead of server_url in the mcp tool.
Write app-server code that connects internally, converts MCP tool lists to function definitions, and relays calls.

questions.explanation:
No public exposure and no custom relay code are decisive. OpenAI’s Secure MCP Tunnel connects local or private MCP servers to OpenAI products without public exposure. Run the tunnel client and use tunnel_id instead of server_url in Responses API.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: IP restrictions do not remove the public endpoint, violating the exposure prohibition.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The server stays private but the model no longer chooses tools and arguments.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It preserves the existing MCP server and mcp tool approach without exposure. The tradeoff is installing and operating the tunnel client.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Privacy and model tool choice are retained, but custom discovery conversion and relay code violate minimal changes.

Tunnel setup and authentication are covered by the separate Secure MCP Tunnel guide. This question concerns choosing the connection method.

**References**: [OpenAI MCP and Connectors › Secure MCP Tunnel](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-connectors-mcp)

questions.title: Creating statistics and charts from an uploaded CSV
questions.prompt:
A Claude API service returns monthly sales totals, growth rates, and chart images from uploaded CSVs. pandas and matplotlib are sufficient. Requirements:

- Calculate with **code, not model arithmetic**.
- Minimize **application code changes**.
- Do **not place user data at public URLs**.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Pass the CSV through container_upload to the code_execution server tool and retrieve generated charts by file_id.
Implement statistics and charts in the app server with libraries and ask the model only to explain the results.
Publish the CSV at a readable public link for an internal processing service to download and process, then pass results to the model.
Paste the CSV into the prompt for step-by-step model arithmetic and have the model write SVG chart code.

questions.explanation:
Code-based calculation, minimal changes, and no public URLs are decisive. Claude code execution runs in a sandbox on Anthropic infrastructure. Files API CSV uploads enter through container_upload, and files saved by code under $OUTPUT_DIR return as downloadable file_id values. The sandbox has no internet or runtime package installation, but preinstalled pandas and matplotlib cover this task.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: A server tool avoids building an execution environment, performs calculations in code, and receives data through Files API.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It computes in code without public exposure, but adds application implementation and operation for statistics and charts.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It computes in code but publicly exposes user data; link creation and integration also add code.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Changes are small, but step-by-step arithmetic is still performed by the model, violating code-based calculation.

Downloadable files must be generated by code execution or skills; original Files API uploads cannot be downloaded again. Billing is based on execution time, and requests containing files may incur execution-time charges even without a tool call.

**References**: [Claude Code execution tool › Upload and analyze files](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/code-execution-tool) · [Claude Files API › Using file\_id in Messages](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/files)

questions.title: Displaying web-search citations and restricting domains
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI Responses API web_search feature explains regulatory changes. Requirements:

- Sources are **visible and clickable beside each claim**.
- Evidence is linked **at sentence level**.
- Results come **only from designated trusted domains**.

Select TWO implementations.

options.text: Store citations only in internal audit logs, without displaying them.
Render answer-text url_citation annotations as prominent clickable links.
Display every URL in web_search_call.action.sources as one reference list below the answer.
Set filters.blocked_domains to exclude a list of untrusted sites.
Set filters.allowed_domains to restrict searches to trusted domains.

questions.explanation:
Visible clickable citations and trusted-domain-only retrieval are decisive. OpenAI requires clearly visible, clickable inline citations when showing web-search results or derived information. url_citation provides URL, title, and citation-span start/end indices. Responses API web_search supports filters with allowlists and blocklists of up to 100 domains each.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Stored citations are invisible to users.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Links tied to sentence spans satisfy the first two requirements.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: sources lists all visited URLs, often more than those cited. A footer list loses sentence-level linkage.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: A blocklist excludes only named domains and permits all others, violating trusted-only retrieval.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: An allowlist restricts retrieval to designated trusted domains.

search_context_size controls the amount of search material supplied to the model, not citation count. Domain filtering is unavailable in Chat Completions search.

**References**: [OpenAI Web search › Output and citations](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-web-search) · [OpenAI Web search › Domain filtering](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-web-search)

questions.title: Matching requirements to tool types
questions.prompt: Match five requirements to tool types. One type is unused. Distinguish functionality the application must implement from provider-supplied tools.

options.text: Structured outputs with an output schema
A server-executed web-fetch tool
A remote MCP server connection
Model fine-tuning
A server-executed web-search tool
Function calling executed by developer code

items.text: Check today’s changes to regulations with sources.
Query an internal-only order database and filter results by requester permissions.
Read and summarize the body of a public report URL pasted by the user.
Integrate an existing tool collection exposed by a partner SaaS without implementing it yourself.
Return fixed fields that the receiving parser can read.

questions.explanation:

| Requirement | Match | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| 1: Current regulations | {{option:e}} | Server web search supplies current information and sources without app-side search implementation. |
| 2: Internal DB with permission filtering | {{option:f}} | Developer-executed client functions handle internal access and authorization. |
| 3: Read a supplied URL | {{option:b}} | Web fetch retrieves a specified URL. Search is for unknown addresses. |

questions.title: Combining internal rules with current web evidence
questions.prompt:
A Gemini API assistant must answer using internal rules already in a File Search store and current public-web information. Gemini documentation says File Search cannot share a request with Google Search grounding or URL context. Requirements:

- Display evidence **separately by source type**.
- Keep the **existing File Search store**, without reloading documents differently.
- Use **at most two model calls** per question.
- Web information must be **current at question time**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Use one Google Search request with full policy PDFs inline, displaying source types separately.
Retrieve current web information with Google Search, then pass its summary into a File Search request for the final answer, distinguishing source types.
Use one File Search request and periodically have staff add web summaries to the store, distinguishing source types.
Make separate File Search and Google Search requests, then combine their answers with a third call, distinguishing source types.

questions.explanation:
Tool incompatibility, two calls, store preservation, and current information are decisive. Separate requests are necessary; with only two calls, one output must feed the next. The app distinguishes the first response’s url_citation from the second response’s file_citation annotations.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It obtains web evidence but bypasses the existing store with inline rules and increases input tokens each request.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Two sequential requests satisfy tool compatibility, the call cap, store reuse, and current web access. The tradeoff is serial latency.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: One call suffices, but web information lags behind the collection schedule.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It separates tools and sources but needs a prohibited third synthesis call.

Gemini 3 and 4 can combine built-in tools and custom function calling in one request, but that combination is not used here. Imported File Search store data remains until deleted.

**References**: [Gemini File Search › Combining with other tools](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/file-search) · [Gemini Grounding with Google Search › Citations](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/google-search) · [Gemini Tools overview](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/tools)

questions.title: A configuration meeting Requirement 1
questions.prompt: Which configuration meets [Requirement 1]?

questions.title: Input design for a 480-page PDF with scanned pages
questions.prompt:
A Claude API internal-manual Q&A feature uses a model with a 200k-token context window. Its single 480-page PDF has dense tables and figures, with some scanned pages lacking text layers. Sending it whole fails or exhausts context. Requirements:

- Each request succeeds within **page, request-size, and context limits**.
- Read **tables, figures, and scanned content**.
- Pay no input cost for **irrelevant sections**.
- Users enter only questions, **not page ranges**.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Split the PDF by chapter or section, estimate tokens, and send only question-relevant sections as document blocks.
Split into five pieces of at most 100 pages, send five requests per question, and combine answers in the app.
Extract only the text layer and use text chunks, accepting only table and figure content represented there.
Send only the first 100 pages containing contents and overview, requiring users to specify later page ranges.

questions.explanation:
Successful bounded requests and no irrelevant-section costs are decisive. Claude PDF requests allow 32MB and 600 pages, reduced to 100 pages for context windows below 1M tokens. Each page has roughly 1,500–3,000 text tokens plus image tokens, so dense PDFs can exhaust context before the page limit. Documentation recommends splitting large PDFs and estimating tokens. Pages are also processed as images, allowing scanned content.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Relevant bounded sections preserve multimodal content and avoid irrelevant input. The tradeoff is question-to-section selection logic.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Requests may fit limits and read content, but all 480 pages are processed for every question, including irrelevant sections.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Input is lighter but scanned pages without text layers and figures are lost.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Limits and costs are controlled, but users must specify page ranges.

Repeated PDFs can use Files API file_id references to reduce request size. Limits vary by platform; Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud support only base64 input.

**References**: [Claude PDF support › Support requirements](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/pdf-support) · [Claude PDF support › Optimize PDF processing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/pdf-support)

- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Fewer results reduce latency and tokens with the explicitly accepted quality tradeoff.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Citations identify source files but lack the supporting chunk text required for audit.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Including results allows evidence chunks to be recorded.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It may reduce generation time but changes the validated model.

questions.prompt:

- Include **evidence from scans** in citations.
- Query **both document types together**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Send scans unchanged as document blocks and enable citations: {enabled: true} for all documents.
OCR scanned contracts into plain-text documents and enable citations on every document block in the request.
Use one cited request for text PDFs and a separate uncited request for scans, combining answers in the app.
Send all contracts without citations and prompt for supporting sentences and page numbers.

questions.explanation:
Scan evidence, joint querying, and citation pointers are decisive. Claude cannot cite scanned PDFs without extractable text. Citations must be enabled for all documents in a request or none, not selectively. OCR converts scans into text documents so all can be queried with citations together.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The request can be sent, but scans lack text and their evidence cannot return as citations.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Text-converted scans become citable in the same request. Tradeoffs are OCR cost and errors; plain-text citations use char_location rather than page numbers.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It separates the document types and leaves scanned evidence uncited.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Prompted page references are model-generated text, not citation pointers.

questions.title: Uploaded PDFs disappear after three days
questions.prompt:
A Gemini document Q&A app cannot find a Files API PDF three days after upload. Documents change quarterly and users query them for weeks or months. Requirements:

- Continue querying **the same document beyond three days**.
- Avoid **recurring work such as pre-expiry re-uploading**.
- Do **not resend the full PDF for every question**.
- Operate **no new vector database** with the two-person team.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Schedule re-uploads before expiration and query each new URI.
Attach the full PDF inline as base64 from app storage for every question.
Embed page chunks in a new self-managed vector database and send only retrieved chunks.
Import the uploaded PDF into a File Search store and query the store thereafter.

questions.explanation:
Long-term access, no recurring upload, and no new vector DB are decisive. Gemini Files API originals expire after 48 hours. Imported File Search data remains until deletion, and embeddings remain until deleted or the model is retired. Existing uploads use importFile; new files can use uploadToFileSearchStore. Both are asynchronous operations whose completion must be checked.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Access continues but requires prohibited recurring uploads.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It avoids expiry but resends the entire PDF each question.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Retrieval reduces input but adds an embedding pipeline and vector database to operate.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Persistent managed-store data and selective retrieval satisfy all four requirements.

questions.title: Rescanning to reduce PDF recognition errors
questions.prompt:
A Gemini API team sees errors answering questions about table structure and seal positions in scanned contracts. Most affected pages are **rotated or blurred**. Someone proposes rescanning from 300dpi to 600dpi. Constraints:

- One person rescans, so **minimize pages requiring rescanning**.
- Do **not increase PDF upload time**.
- Continue answering about **visual-only page information** such as tables and seal positions.

Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Rescan every page at 600dpi to increase page-image resolution nearly threefold.
Correct rotated pages and rescan only blurred pages, leaving all others at current resolution.
Reduce every page to about 150dpi to shrink uploads.
Extract text with OCR and query only text, omitting page images.

questions.explanation:
Minimal rescanning, unchanged upload time, and visual queries are decisive. Gemini recommends correctly oriented, nonblurry pages. Page images larger than 3072 x 3072 are downscaled preserving aspect ratio, while those smaller than 768 x 768 are enlarged; each page counts as 258 tokens. A4 at 300dpi already exceeds 3,000 pixels on its long side, so 600dpi barely changes the image ultimately supplied to the model.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It greatly increases work and upload size, while resolution limits largely erase the model-input benefit.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It fixes the actual orientation and focus causes only where needed without expanding rescanning or upload size.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Uploads shrink but visual detail may worsen, and fixed 258-token page accounting gives no token savings.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Text remains queryable, but seals and table layouts lose their image representation.

For a single PDF page plus a text prompt, Gemini recommends placing the prompt after the page.

**References**: [Document processing › Technical details](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/document-processing) · [Document processing › Best practices](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/document-processing)

questions.title: Preparing embeddings for Claude-based internal search
questions.prompt: A team building internal document search with Claude API is choosing how to create vectors. It compares document and query embeddings to select nearest documents. Select TWO statements matching Anthropic documentation.

options.text: Specify a Claude model ID at Anthropic’s embedding endpoint to obtain vectors without choosing another provider.
Anthropic provides no embedding model of its own; documentation points to Voyage AI.
Voyage embeddings have unit length, so dot product equals cosine similarity.
Document and query embeddings must use the same input_type to be comparable.
Voyage embeddings are unnormalized, so each vector must be divided by its norm before cosine comparison.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Claude models are not offered as embedding-vector endpoints, hence the external-provider guidance.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: A separate embedding provider is the documented starting point.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Normalization makes dot-product ranking equivalent to cosine ranking.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Different document and query input_type values are expected and demonstrated.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: Vectors are already unit-normalized; the example selects nearest documents with a dot product and no additional division.

questions.title: Evaluating image and PDF input limits
questions.prompt: A developer handling image and document input across three platforms is checking the following statements against official documentation. Mark Yes or No.

items.text: A Claude API request with 25 images must resize a 3000-pixel-wide image to no more than 2000 pixels because the request exceeds 20 images.
OpenAI automatically reduces images exceeding the per-image patch limit, so sending without prior resizing will not cause rejection.
A 40-page PDF sent to a Gemini 3 model counts as approximately 10,320 input tokens at 258 per page, reported under IMAGE modality.

1. **Yes**: Claude Vision allows 100 images per API request for 200k-context models and 600 for other models. When a request has more than 20 images, no image dimension may exceed 2000 pixels, so the 3000-pixel image must be resized.
2. **No**: OpenAI says images exceeding the 30,000-patch per-image limit are rejected rather than automatically reduced. Resize them before calling; the limit applies independently to each image.
3. **Yes**: Gemini counts each document page as 258 tokens, giving 10,320 for 40 pages. Gemini 3 reports page-image tokens under IMAGE rather than DOCUMENT.
4. **Yes**: Claude Files API uploads can be referenced by file_id across multiple turns or agent calls without resending base64.

items.text: Call responses.create with vector_store_ids in file_search and file_search_call.results in include.
Add the file to the vector store.
Inspect returned search results and adjust max_num_results.
Upload the file through Files API with purpose assistants and obtain its file ID.
Repeatedly inspect the store’s file list until the file status becomes completed.

questions.title: Analyzing 1,800 images in one request
questions.prompt:
An OpenAI Responses API request for crack detection contains 1,800 construction-site frames, about 0.4MB each and 720MB total, and is rejected. Requirements:

- Send frames at **original resolution** to preserve tiny cracks.
- Keep the **current model**.
- Combine results into one table by frame number.

Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Set detail to low for every image to reduce the number of images counted in a request.
Combine six frames into each grid image, reducing the count to 300 in one request.
Split frames so every request has at most 1,500 images and 512MB payload, then combine results.
Upload file IDs to reduce the request body and keep all 1,800 images in one request.

questions.explanation:
Original resolution, unchanged model, and frame-number aggregation are decisive. OpenAI allows at most 1,500 images and 512MB total payload per request. Both limits are exceeded. Two requests of 900 images each are about 360MB apiece and satisfy both.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: confusion between controls)**: detail changes processing granularity, not image-count limits. 1,800 remains invalid.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Grids reduce count but shrink frames within composites and blur small cracks, violating original resolution.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It preserves both limits, original resolution, and the model, then aggregates by frame ID.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: confusion between mechanisms)**: File IDs avoid inline data but do not change the image-count limit.

questions.title: Drawing Gemini bounding boxes on the original photo
questions.prompt:
A Gemini API feature locates missing safety rails in a 4032 x 3024 original photo and overlays boxes on that **original**. To reduce transfer size, the model receives a 1344 x 1008 copy and returns box_2d values [250, 100, 750, 400]. Requirements:

- Draw at the **correct original-resolution location**.
- Convert using **only the returned values**, without another model call.
- Express the box as top-left (x, y) – bottom-right (x, y) pixels.

Which box is appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Original-resolution placement and direct conversion are decisive. Gemini returns [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] normalized to 0–1000. Multiply by original dimensions regardless of the submitted resized copy, using height for y and width for x.

Calculation: ymin = 250 × 3024 / 1000 = 756; xmin = 100 × 4032 / 1000 ≈ 403; ymax = 750 × 3024 / 1000 = 2268; xmax = 400 × 4032 / 1000 ≈ 1613.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It follows the documented order and scales each axis by the original dimension.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: factual error)**: It treats values as [xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax], swapping axes.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It scales by the 1344 x 1008 copy and applies those pixels to the original, producing a smaller box shifted toward the upper-left.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: x is correct, but y also uses the width factor 4.032, misplacing vertical coordinates on a 3024-pixel-high image.

**References**: [Image understanding › Object detection](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/image-understanding)

questions.title: Reusing claim photos across turns under ZDR

An insurer with a Zero Data Retention agreement uses Claude API to organize claim photos. Users upload five JPEGs of about 5MB each, and the model must **reinspect the same photos across multiple turns**. Sending base64 every turn exceeds a request-size limit. Requirements:

Which method is most appropriate?

- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Payload shrinks, but later turns cannot inspect original photo content.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Public image hosting violates the third condition.

- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Accuracy and size requirements are met, but maximum resolution for every photo unnecessarily increases tokens and latency, from the default 1,120 to 2,240 tokens per image.

The correct approach requires selecting which photos need small-detail resolution and re-uploading expired files from application originals after 48 hours. Upgraded photos still incur more tokens and latency.
