questions.title: Defining success criteria for summarization
questions.prompt: Before improving customer-conversation summaries, a team defines success criteria for before-and-after evaluation using an evaluation set and automated grading. Summaries appear immediately in an agent’s screen. Which criterion best matches Anthropic’s requirements of specificity, measurability, achievability, and relevance?

options.text: Three teammates’ manually assigned satisfaction scores average at least 4.5 out of 5.
All summaries contain all five key items, have zero factual errors, and never exceed one second of latency.
Adopt the version improving key-item recall by at least 5 percentage points, ignoring length and latency.
At least 90% of summaries contain four of five key items, stay within 400 tokens, and meet p95 latency of three seconds or less.

questions.explanation:
Anthropic recommends specific, measurable, achievable, relevant criteria and multidimensional assessment, such as quality alongside response time. Immediate display to agents makes length and latency relevant too.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Numeric subjective scores require manual grading, conflict with repeated automated comparison, and omit length and latency, weakening measurability and relevance.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Perfect coverage, zero errors, and an absolute latency ceiling are unrealistic, violating achievability.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Recall is measurable but one-dimensional, omitting relevant screen-length and latency requirements.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Ratios, counts, tokens, and latency quantify a multidimensional quality, length, and response-time standard.

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Success criteria](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

questions.title: Building a weekly before-and-after evaluation set
questions.prompt:
A team creates an evaluation set for weekly prompt deployments. The model is fixed. Requirements:

- Reuse the **same set weekly**.
- Only **one grader** is available.
- Include **edge cases** such as empty, very long, and ambiguous input.
- Reflect the **production input distribution**.

Which setup is most appropriate?

options.text: Build about 1,000 automatically gradable inputs following production logs, including selected edge cases.
Choose 50 sophisticated inputs for careful weekly manual grading and per-case notes.
Draw 100 new random production-log inputs each week and manually grade them.
Automatically grade 1,000 model-generated fictional inputs without using production logs.

questions.explanation:
Repeatability, one-person capacity, edge coverage, and production representativeness are decisive. Anthropic recommends real-task distributions and automated grading where possible, preferring many automatically graded cases even with slightly weaker signal over few manually graded cases. Include empty or nonexistent inputs, long inputs, and ambiguities difficult even for humans. OpenAI likewise recommends production-like data and treats dataset bias as an antipattern.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Automation supports weekly runs with one person, while production distribution and edge cases are covered.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Strong signal comes with recurring manual burden and narrower edge coverage.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Random production samples rarely cover rare edges and changing weekly inputs prevent same-set comparisons while requiring manual grading.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Automation is repeatable but entirely synthetic inputs do not reflect production distribution.

**References**: [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Design evaluations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests) · [OpenAI Evaluation best practices › Dataset anti-patterns](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices)

questions.title: Preparing for OpenAI Evals retirement
questions.prompt:
A team using the OpenAI Evals dashboard for deployment comparisons receives a retirement notice: evaluations will become read-only before shutdown. Requirements:

- Continue **automated before-and-after comparisons** for every deployment.
- Preserve **evaluation-set and grading-criteria history**.
- Compare by the **same standards after retirement**.

Select TWO preparations.

options.text: Use Evals until read-only, then switch to manual inspection of representative cases at deployment.
Move datasets and grading criteria into repository files and code, running identical standards in an internal evaluation harness.
Move only datasets to another hosted service and use its default grading template.
Archive result screenshots, then start a new evaluation set for future automated comparisons.
Secure existing datasets and results before read-only status, then replay historical inputs in the new harness to verify score reproduction.

questions.explanation:
Automated continuity, preserved history, and unchanged standards are decisive. OpenAI announces Evals retirement following a read-only period; evaluation guidance treats testing as continuous for every change and recommends automated grading. Moving both data and grading outside the platform and validating score reproduction preserves continuity.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Manual inspection cannot continue automated deployment comparisons.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Owned files and code preserve the same standards independently of platform retirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Automation continues but default grading changes standards and loses grading history.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Screenshots are not dataset and rubric history, and a new set cannot provide like-for-like historical comparison.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Securing data and reproducing historical scores verifies unchanged standards.

The retirement notice links migration guidance for Promptfoo. It does not specify detailed export procedures, so confirm data-retrieval methods through official documentation or support.

**References**: [OpenAI Evaluation getting started](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-getting-started) · [OpenAI Evaluation best practices › Continuous evaluation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices) · [OpenAI Deprecations › Evals platform](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations)

questions.title: Reducing overnight batch waste from validation errors
questions.prompt:
A team submits 100,000 prior-day conversation summaries nightly through Claude Message Batches. Yesterday, after hours of processing, about 2% were errored with invalid_request_error and could only be rerun tonight. Requirements:

- Results are needed **within 24 hours**.
- Preserve the **50% batch discount**.
- Transient server errors can be **resent without modifying their bodies**.

What is the best improvement for the next run?

options.text: Split into batches of 1,000 and inspect each completed batch to discover errors sooner and resubmit only affected batches.
Validate a small sample of representative request shapes through Messages API before submission, then identify invalid_request_error cases by custom_id, fix, and resubmit.
Collect every errored request regardless of type and resend unchanged in the following night’s batch.
Call all 100,000 requests through ordinary Messages API first, then submit passing ones as a batch.

questions.explanation:
The 24-hour deadline, batch discount, and unchanged transient retries are decisive. Claude validates batch params asynchronously, so validation failures appear only after completion. Documentation recommends checking each request shape through ordinary Messages API beforehand. Results are unordered and must be matched by custom_id. Fix invalid_request_error bodies before resubmission; other errors can be retried unchanged. Errored requests are not billed.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Smaller batches isolate failures but validation still arrives after completion, leaving the cause and deadline pressure.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Small prevalidation catches request-shape problems, and later handling branches by error type.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: approach for a different error)**: Server failures may be retried unchanged, but invalid_request_error repeats without repair.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Full standard-price duplication defeats the intended 50% batch savings.

**References**: [Batch processing › Batch results](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing) · [Batch processing › Best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing)

questions.title: Improving shared-prefix cache hits in Claude batches
questions.prompt:
A Claude Message Batch processes 3,000 classifications sharing a 12k-token prefix. They fit one batch’s 100,000-request or 256MB limit. cache_control is at the prefix end, but near-simultaneous processing attempts reads before the first write completes, causing poor hits. Requirements:

- Finish **within 48 hours**; since each batch can take 24 hours, submit at most **two sequential batches**.
- Combine **batch and cache discounts**.
- Keep the **same prefix** for all 3,000 requests.

Which method is most appropriate?

options.text: Set a one-hour cache TTL and submit all 3,000 requests together.
Submit ten batches of 300 sequentially, each after the previous finishes.
First process one request with the shared prefix and one-hour cache as a batch to warm it, then submit the rest in one batch.
Use synchronous ordinary Messages API calls and directly control prefix-reuse order.

questions.explanation:
The 48-hour/two-batch cap and combined discounts are decisive. Claude cache entries become available after the first response starts, and batch cache hits are best-effort. Documentation recommends first sending one request with the shared prefix and a one-hour cache block, then submitting the rest after completion. One-hour caching is preferred because batches can exceed five minutes. All 3,000 fit the 100,000-request or 256MB batch cap.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Longer TTL does not fix simultaneous reads before the first write.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Ten sequential batches exceed the two-batch cap and may exceed 48 hours.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Warming first improves hit likelihood while preserving two sequential batches and both discounts.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Cache hits are easier to control, but the batch discount is lost.

The tradeoff is waiting for the warm-up request before submitting the remainder, up to 48 hours worst case, and one-hour cache writes costing twice base input.

**References**: [Prompt caching › Batch usage](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Batch processing › Using prompt caching with Message Batches](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing)

questions.title: Why Claude cache hits dropped to zero after deployment
questions.prompt:
A Claude Sonnet 5.5 support app sends a long system prompt and 12 tool definitions. cache_control is on the final tool, final system block, and latest user message. Deployment changes:

- Image blocks are added for photo attachments, about 5% of requests.
- tool_choice selects a specific tool when needed, about 8%.
- Citations can be enabled, about 10%.
- Tool definitions now follow internal hash-map iteration order.

Monitoring shows **almost all requests have cache_read_input_tokens of 0 and high cache_creation_input_tokens**. What should be fixed first?

options.text: Route image requests separately so images cannot affect earlier cache sections.
Fix tool_choice to one value in requests selecting tools.
Keep citations consistently enabled or disabled within each conversation.
Emit tool definitions in the same order every request so definitions remain identical.

questions.explanation:
The key clue is that three changes affect only 5–10% of requests while nearly all have zero reads. Claude caching follows tools → system → messages, requires exact prefix matches, and changes invalidate their level and subsequent levels. Tool changes invalidate all three. Image and tool_choice changes affect messages only; citation toggles affect system and messages. Those limited changes cannot explain almost universal zero reads, whereas changing tool order at the earliest level can.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Images genuinely invalidate message blocks, but cannot explain zero reads in most requests without photos.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: tool_choice also affects messages only and not most requests without forced tools.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Citations invalidate system/messages but leave tools valid and affect only a minority.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Varying tool definitions breaks the earliest prefix and all three cache points. Stable ordering restores reuse.

**References**: [Prompt caching › What invalidates the cache](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)

questions.title: Reducing OpenAI total response time
questions.prompt:
A GPT-5.6 Responses API contract-analysis feature sequentially calls (1) issue-clause extraction, (2) party/date extraction, and (3) risk summarization. The first two are independent; the third needs both. Summaries are about 800 tokens, though users need only three key lines. Requirements:

- Reduce **total completion time**.
- Keep the **validated model**.
- Do **not remove analysis rules** from prompts.

Select TWO actions consistent with OpenAI latency guidance.

options.text: Stream summary output to show early text sooner.
Request at most three lines of key issues to reduce generated tokens.
Halve each prompt’s analysis-rule explanations to reduce input.
Use a smaller model for all three stages.
Run (1) and (2) concurrently, then pass both results to (3).

questions.explanation:
Total time, unchanged model, and retained rules are decisive. OpenAI says reducing output tokens reduces latency approximately proportionally and independent stages should run in parallel. Halving input may improve latency only 1–5%; streaming instead reduces perceived waiting.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: approach for a different objective)**: It improves perceived waiting, not time until the full response completes.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Generation time largely scales with output tokens, so shorter summaries reduce total time.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: The expected latency gain is only 1–5% and required analysis rules are removed.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Smaller models may be faster but violate the model constraint.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Concurrent independent extraction takes less time than their sequential sum.

**References**: [OpenAI Latency optimization › Seven principles](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization)

questions.title: Gemini implicit caching never hits
questions.prompt:
A Gemini 3.6 Flash support feature sends a 3,200-token system prompt, followed by user-specific questions and history. Requests arrive several times per second, but usage never shows cached tokens. Another 1,500 tokens of common reference material currently follow the user question. Requirements:

- **Minimal code changes**.
- Keep the **validated model**.
- **Minimize input cost**.

Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Move common references directly after the system prompt to create a prefix of at least 4,096 tokens, followed by user-specific content.
Switch to Gemini 2.5 Flash with a 2,048-token minimum so the current prefix qualifies.
Add about 1,000 tokens of example responses to exceed 4,096, leaving references where they are.
Create an explicit cache of the system prompt and references and change calls to reference it.

questions.explanation:
Minimal changes, same model, and minimum cost are decisive. Gemini implicit caching is enabled by default from 2.5 onward. Gemini 3.6 Flash needs at least 4,096 tokens, so 3,200 does not qualify. Documentation recommends large common content first and similar-prefix requests close together; usage reports cache hits.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Reordering existing reference tokens crosses the threshold without adding tokens, leaving variable content last.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It meets a minimum but changes the validated model.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It may qualify with little code, but adds unnecessary input tokens and cost.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Explicit-cache creation and references require more code. Explicit caching is also unsupported in Interactions API and Gemini 4 Argon onward.

**References**: [Context caching › Implicit caching](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching) · [Context caching › Explicit caching](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching)

questions.title: An inconsistent model grader for open-ended answers
questions.prompt:
A team automatically grades service answers using “Assign overall quality from 1–5,” but identical answers receive varying scores. Results will later be compared with human labels. Requirements:

- Produce **specific, measurable judgments**.
- Use **one model call per answer**, automatically without human intervention.
- Keep the **validated high-capability grading model**.
- Prioritize **score stability over grading cost**.

Select TWO improvements consistent with OpenAI and Anthropic guidance.

options.text: Replace overall scores with concrete criterion-level pass/fail judgments or pairwise comparison.
Keep overall 1–5 scoring, grade each answer five times, and average.
Switch to a smaller faster grader and call once per answer.
Have the grader first explain evidence for each criterion, then judge based on that evidence.
Have humans assign final scores for unstable cases and keep model scores for the rest.

questions.explanation:
Specific outputs, one automatic call, and the same strong model are decisive. OpenAI says models discriminate between options better than performing open-ended generation, recommending pairwise comparisons, pass/fail, and concrete rubrics. Reasoning before scoring improves evaluation. Anthropic similarly recommends concrete correct/incorrect outputs and reasoning before the score.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Concrete binary judgments or pairwise comparisons reduce the ambiguous scale while retaining one call.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Averaging may help but preserves ambiguity and raises calls to five.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It saves cost and time but changes the validated stronger model; OpenAI recommends the most capable available grader.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Evidence before judgment ties scoring to criteria more consistently. Extra tokens are acceptable because stability outranks cost.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Human adjudication may stabilize results but violates unattended automation and leaves the grader’s inconsistency unresolved.

**References**: [OpenAI Evaluation best practices › LLM-as-a-judge](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices) · [Define success criteria and build evaluations › Grading evals](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests)

questions.title: Matching optimization techniques to conditions
questions.prompt: Match situations 1–5 to techniques a–f. One technique is unused. All are real techniques; choose based on each situation’s constraints.

options.text: Asynchronous bulk processing
Cheaper reuse of identical input segments
Sequential delivery of partial responses
Use a lighter model tier
Instructions reducing output length
Upgrade to the highest-capability model

items.text: Label 100,000 overnight customer inquiries; results are needed after staff arrive next day, and per-item cost should be minimized.
Every call begins with the same 8,000-token support instructions, followed by varying questions; reduce input cost and processing time.
Users stare at a blank chat screen until a long summary completes, but total generation time cannot change.
Verbose answers take too long to generate although two or three sentences suffice.
High-volume simple labeling loses users when slow; evaluation confirms a lower-reasoning tier meets accuracy requirements.

questions.explanation:
| Situation | Technique | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | {{option:a}}: Asynchronous batch processing | Bulk work does not need immediate results. Claude Batch costs 50% of standard pricing and completes within up to 24 hours. |
| 2 | {{option:b}}: Prompt caching | Repeated calls share a long prefix. Cache reads cost less than base input. |
| 3 | {{option:c}}: Streaming | Total generation time is fixed; streaming reduces perceived waiting, which OpenAI identifies as its strongest use. |
| 4 | {{option:e}}: Shorter output instructions | Generation time is roughly proportional to output tokens, so shorter sufficient output reduces total time. |
| 5 | {{option:d}}: Lighter model tier | Smaller models are generally faster and cheaper, and this task already passed quality evaluation on the lower tier. |
| Unused | {{option:f}}: Highest-tier model | Increased latency and cost do not match any listed objective. |

Both situations 3 and 4 concern waiting. Fixed total time points to streaming in 3; sufficient short content points to fewer output tokens in 4.

**References**: [Claude Batch processing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing) · [Claude Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [OpenAI Latency optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization)

questions.title: Sequencing OpenAI Batch API processing
questions.prompt: A team is moving overnight summarization of prior-day inquiries from Responses API calls to Batch API. Arrange the steps from input-file creation through matching results to original inquiries.

items.text: Check batch status until completed.
Create a JSONL file with custom_id, method, url, and body on each request line.
Download output_file_id and match results to original inquiries using custom_id.
Create the batch with input_file_id, endpoint, and completion_window.
Upload the input file through Files API with purpose batch and obtain its ID.

questions.explanation:
The documented sequence is JSONL preparation, upload, batch creation, status checks, and result retrieval. Each stage produces the next stage’s input.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | (2) Create JSONL | A file must exist before upload. | Each line contains custom_id, method, url, and body. |
| 2 | (5) Upload through Files API | The file produces an input file ID. | Set purpose to batch. |
| 3 | (4) Create the batch | Use the uploaded ID as input_file_id. | completion_window supports only 24h. |
| 4 | (1) Check status | The batch must exist first. | States include validating, in_progress, finalizing, and completed. |
| 5 | (3) Download and match output | Completed status makes results available. | Output order may differ; match by custom_id. |

Failures are available through error_file_id. A batch unfinished within 24 hours becomes expired; only completed requests are billed.

**References**: [OpenAI Batch API › How it works](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch) · [OpenAI Batch API › Retrieving results](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch)

questions.title: Overnight processing meeting Requirement 1
questions.prompt: Which overnight processing approach satisfies [Requirement 1]?
questions.context:
**[Company]** Bareun Telecom operates telecom contact centers and summarizes conversations using OpenAI Responses API and GPT-5.6.

**[Existing environment]** Every summary request contains about 6,000 tokens of shared rules plus conversation logs. Daytime summaries run synchronously immediately after calls. Overnight, about 200,000 prior-day conversations are summarized again. Each overnight request line, including rules, is about 30KB. Daytime traffic already consumes most synchronous rate-limit capacity.

**[Requirement 1]** Overnight results are needed only by the next morning. They must not affect synchronous limits, and cost should be minimized.

**[Requirement 2]** Daytime prompt v2 moves fixed rules forward to improve cache hits. Compare quality using 3,000 conversations, including 300 with human reference summaries. Do not affect production summaries. Evaluation spending must stay within 60% of synchronous-call cost, results are needed for a meeting in about 36 hours, and model-grader results must be trustworthy. Estimate v2 economics including its first cache-write cost.

options.text: Run many dedicated overnight workers making synchronous Responses API calls for all 200,000 cases.
Split into at least 31 files of about 6,500 requests each to satisfy both count and size limits, submit batches, and match by custom_id.
Split into four 50,000-request files, submit batches, and merge by custom_id.
Combine 20 conversations per synchronous request and process those requests sequentially overnight.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are separate synchronous capacity, minimum cost, next-morning results, and 30KB per line. OpenAI Batch has a 24-hour window, costs 50% less, and uses a separate rate-limit pool. Each input file permits at most 50,000 requests and 200MB and targets one model. At 30KB per line, roughly 6,600 fit 200MB, so size binds first. Match results using custom_id because order can differ.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: It may finish overnight but consumes synchronous limits and costs twice batch processing.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Size- and count-safe splitting uses separate capacity and the 50% discount, with ID matching.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Count fits, but each file is about 1.5GB, exceeding 200MB.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Fewer calls still use synchronous capacity without batch discounts, and multi-conversation requests complicate matching.

Check the model-specific queued-prompt-token limit before submitting all 31 files at once. Unfinished batches expire after 24 hours, billing only completed requests.

**References**: [OpenAI Batch API › Rate limits](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch) · [OpenAI Batch API › Batch input file](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch) · [OpenAI Batch API › Retrieving results](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch)

questions.title: A comparison plan meeting Requirement 2
questions.prompt: Which comparison plan satisfies [Requirement 2]?
questions.context:
**[Company]** Bareun Telecom operates telecom contact centers and summarizes conversations using OpenAI Responses API and GPT-5.6.

**[Existing environment]** Every summary request contains about 6,000 tokens of shared rules plus conversation logs. Daytime summaries run synchronously immediately after calls. Overnight, about 200,000 prior-day conversations are summarized again. Each overnight request line, including rules, is about 30KB. Daytime traffic already consumes most synchronous rate-limit capacity.

**[Requirement 1]** Overnight results are needed only by the next morning. They must not affect synchronous limits, and cost should be minimized.

**[Requirement 2]** Daytime prompt v2 moves fixed rules forward to improve cache hits. Compare quality using 3,000 conversations, including 300 with human reference summaries. Do not affect production summaries. Evaluation spending must stay within 60% of synchronous-call cost, results are needed for a meeting in about 36 hours, and model-grader results must be trustworthy. Estimate v2 economics including its first cache-write cost.

options.text: Send 5% of production to v2 for a week, compare repeat inquiries and agent complaints with human quality reviews, and price first cache writes at 1.25 times and reads at 0.1 times input.
Run all 3,000 evaluations on v1 and v2 in batches, trust one model grader alone, and include 1.25-times first writes and 0.1-times reads.
Run all 3,000 evaluations on v1 and v2 in batches, use a grader validated against 300 human labels, and include 1.25-times first writes and 0.1-times reads.
Run all 3,000 evaluations on v1 and v2 synchronously, use a grader validated against 300 human labels, and include 1.25-times first writes and 0.1-times reads.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements isolate production, validate grading, cap cost at 60% of synchronous pricing, meet the meeting deadline, and include first-write cost. OpenAI recommends validating agreement between automated graders and human labels before scaling, using production-like evaluation data. GPT-5.6 onward cache writes cost 1.25 times uncached input and reads 0.1 times. Writing the 6,000-token prefix initially adds 0.25 times base cost, while each read saves 0.9 times; use reuse counts to estimate break-even. Batch costs 50% of synchronous calls and returns within up to 24 hours, fitting the budget and deadline.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Real-traffic evidence comes at the cost of exposing unvalidated v2 regressions to production users.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Budget and timing fit, but no human-label comparison establishes grader trust.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Isolated evaluations meet batch budget and timing, calibrated grading provides trust, and economics include the first write.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Trust and timing fit, but synchronous cost is 100% of baseline, exceeding 60%.

Tradeoffs include building and maintaining the harness, comparing human labels, and waiting up to 24 hours for batch results within the available 36 hours.
